aardvark.context_blurb:
The aardvark is a shy night digger of the African savanna south of the Sahara. Its name is Afrikaans for "earth pig," and people also call it the antbear. Nearly every oddity of its body serves a single trade: breaking into the rock-hard nests of ants and termites and feasting on the insects inside.

At dusk it shuffles out of its den looking as if it were built from spare parts. The aardvark, Orycteropus afer, has a pig's snout, long ears like a rabbit's, a humped back, a heavy kangaroo-style tail and spade-clawed feet, and a big one weighs 60 to 80 kilograms.

Its front claws smash a mound open, and then the aardvark sends in a sticky tongue, thin as a snake and up to 30 centimeters long, that winds down the tunnels and gathers as many as 50,000 insects in a single night. It looks like an anteater, but the likeness is a coincidence. DNA places the aardvark in Afrotheria, an ancient African group whose living members include its closest cousins, the elephants and manatees, along with the little hyraxes. Biologists call this convergent evolution: the same ant-eating tools arose separately in families that are not related.

Its teeth are rootless columns of thousands of thin dentine tubes, which gave its order the name Tubulidentata, "tube-toothed," and they have no enamel at all, so they wear down on top and keep growing from below for life. The aardvark is also a tireless builder that digs a yard of tunnel in about five minutes and keeps carving fresh burrows it never revisits. Those empty burrows shelter warthogs, hyenas, mongooses, owls, pythons and wild dogs, and many of these animals would die in wildfire season without an aardvark hole to hide in, which is why biologists rank it a keystone species.

A strange plant depends on it too. The aardvark cucumber is the only cucumber that buries its fruit, ripening each melon about a foot underground. In a 2025 camera-trap study of seven mammal species, only the aardvark could find the buried melons and dig them up; it eats them for their water and later drops the seeds in its dung, replanting them with fertilizer.

aye-aye.context_blurb:
Found only in the rainforests of Madagascar, the big island off Africa's east coast, the aye-aye is a lemur that comes out at night. With shaggy dark fur, huge eyes, giant leathery ears and long bony fingers, it looks like no other primate on Earth. Nearly every strange part of its body is a tool for a single job: finding grubs hidden inside wood.

Creeping through the trees after dark with round yellow eyes, swiveling ears and a long, skinny middle finger for tapping bark, the aye-aye is the largest nocturnal primate in the world. Its body is about 15 inches long, and its bushy tail is longer still.

It hunts by rapping on the wood with that finger, as fast as eight taps a second, a habit called percussive foraging that no other primate shares, and it listens for the hollow echo that betrays a grub's tunnel under the bark. Inside each huge ear, tall ridges of bone act like a lens, focusing and funneling the faint echo toward the eardrum, along with the tiny sounds of larvae moving in the wood.

Once it hears a hollow, it gnaws through the bark with two long front teeth that, unlike any other primate's, keep growing throughout its life, which is why early naturalists mistook the aye-aye for a rodent. Then it fishes the grub out with its thin finger, doing the job a woodpecker does elsewhere with its beak, because Madagascar has no woodpeckers and the aye-aye evolved to fill that empty role.

That probing middle finger has a ball-and-socket joint at its knuckle, the only one of its kind in any primate hand, so the finger can rotate freely to hook a grub around the bends of a tunnel. Its fingers are so specialized that they are poor at gripping branches, and in 2019 Adam Hartstone-Rose and Edwin Dickinson found how it climbs anyway: a hidden sixth digit, a pseudothumb of bone and cartilage moved by three muscles and even marked with its own fingerprint.

babirusa.context_blurb:
The babirusa is a wild pig of the swampy rainforests of Sulawesi and a few nearby Indonesian islands. It is shy, mostly solitary and a quick runner for its size, and it wallows in mud and even swims between islands. The male's teeth make it one of the strangest-looking mammals alive.

The babirusa takes its name from the Indonesian words babi rusa, "pig-deer," because local people thought the male's curling tusks looked like a deer's antlers, and its nearly hairless gray body adds to the odd look.

The male's upper canines never leave his mouth the normal way: they grow straight up, punch through the skin on top of the snout and curve back over the face toward the forehead. He actually carries four tusks, because a lower pair of canines sweeps upward too, and in fights between males the lower tusks serve as weapons while the snout tusks act more like shields.

The upper tusks never stop growing, and food does nothing to grind them down, so on a rare old male an unworn tusk keeps arcing until it curls round and pierces his own skull. He grows his teeth through his face and, now and then, back into his own head.

binturong.context_blurb:
The binturong, often called the bearcat, is a shaggy, black, slow-moving mammal that lives high in the rainforest trees of South and Southeast Asia. It is neither bear nor cat but a viverrid, a cousin of the civets, and its genus name, Arctictis, is Greek for "bear-weasel." It eats mostly fruit and comes out mainly at night.

The surest way to recognize a binturong is with your nose: this black, cat-sized tree-dweller smells strongly of hot buttered popcorn.

In 2016 a team at Duke University traced the smell to a molecule called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the very compound that gives hot popcorn and freshly cooked jasmine rice their scent, and found it in every sample of binturong urine they tested. When it leaves a tree, a binturong walks headfirst down the trunk, because its hind ankles can turn a full 180 degrees so the claws stay hooked into the bark, and its grasping tail serves as a fifth limb for balance.

That smell posed a puzzle, since popcorn gets the molecule from intense heat, as sugars and amino acids react in the pan. The lead scientist, Christine Drea, wondered how an animal could produce a cooking smell with no cooking at all, and her team believes microbes on its skin, in its fur or in its gut create the compound as the urine flows past.

capybara.context_blurb:
The capybara is a barrel-shaped grazer of the wetlands, rivers and flooded grasslands of South America. It is calm and social, living in family groups that share water holes with caimans, herons and even monkeys. Its body is built for a life spent half in the water and half grazing at the water's edge.

The capybara, Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, is the largest rodent alive, more than four feet long and usually 35 to 66 kilograms, roughly the weight of an adult man; the heaviest wild one on record, a female from Brazil, weighed 91 kilograms.

Like every rodent, it has front incisors that keep growing throughout its life, replacing exactly what the constant grinding of gritty grass wears away, and the word rodent itself comes from the Latin for "to gnaw." Eyes, ears and nostrils all ride high along the top of its head, the same layout a hippo uses, so it can sink until only that strip shows and still see, hear and breathe while hiding from a jaguar. It can even sleep in the water with just its nose poking out.

Grass is hard to digest, so bacteria in its enlarged hindgut break it down, and because the protein and B vitamins those bacteria make would otherwise pass out unabsorbed, the capybara eats its own soft morning droppings to run the food through a second time, the same trick rabbits use.

fossa.context_blurb: The fossa is the top predator of Madagascar, a sleek, cat-like hunter that stalks lemurs through the island's rainforests and dry woodlands. It looks like a cross between a cougar and a mongoose, with a tail nearly as long as its body and semi-retractable claws for climbing. DNA shows the fossa is not a true cat at all; it belongs to a Madagascar-only family of carnivores descended from a single ancestor that drifted across from mainland Africa many millions of years ago.

giant-panda.context_blurb: The giant panda is a black-and-white bear that lives only in cool, misty mountain bamboo forests in central China. Although its gut is still built like a meat-eater's, almost every panda in the wild spends its day doing one thing: eating bamboo, for ten to sixteen hours at a stretch. Pandas are solitary, slow to breed, and a famous worldwide conservation symbol. Scientists study them for the many strange adaptations that let a bear survive on a plant that gives almost no calories.

kangaroo-rat.context_blurb: The kangaroo rat is a small, big-eyed desert rodent of the American Southwest and Mexico that bounds across hot sand on long back legs, like a tiny kangaroo. It is active only at night, lives in burrows it digs itself, and spends most of its life surrounded by seeds and dry heat. Its body is so finely tuned to the desert that it almost never drinks water. The way it manages to live its entire life without a sip is one of the most studied water tricks in all of mammal biology.

lowland-streaked-tenrec.context_blurb:
In the rainforests of Madagascar, a little mammal roots through the leaf litter looking like a hedgehog dressed as a bumblebee. It belongs to an ancient family found only on that island, and it has a trick no other mammal is known to share.

The lowland streaked tenrec is hamster-sized and weighs only about 125 to 280 grams, with black quills banded in yellow, a yellow stripe running down its nose, and a taste for earthworms.

A mother calls to her young in the thick undergrowth by buzzing, without using her voice at all. In the middle of a tenrec's back sits a patch of 7 to 16 special quills in three rows, and the tenrec grinds them against each other to make its high-pitched clicks and buzzes. This is stridulation, the trick crickets and grasshoppers perform with their wings, and no other mammal is known to do it.

Roughly 30 million years ago a single ancestor reached Madagascar by rafting across the sea from Africa on floating vegetation. Its descendants became about 31 living kinds, shrew-like, hedgehog-like, mole-like and even otter-like, but the likeness is convergent evolution: the tenrecs' real cousins are elephants, aardvarks and sea cows.

maned-wolf.context_blurb: The maned wolf is the tallest wild canid on Earth, a long-legged, fox-colored animal that walks the tall-grass savannas of central South America. Despite the name, it is not a true wolf or fox but the only living member of its genus. Maned wolves are solitary, mostly crepuscular, and known for a scent so sharp that people and zoo keepers can smell them long before they see one. Their diet is also unusual for a dog, leaning heavily on a single fruit of the savanna.

musk-ox.context_blurb: The musk ox is a shaggy, cold-adapted grazer of the Arctic tundra of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, and Siberia. It is not actually an ox; it is more closely related to sheep and goats, and it has survived from the ice age almost unchanged while mammoths and giant deer went extinct around it. Musk oxen live in small herds and have a famous group defense against wolves. Their skirts of fur, the longest of any land mammal, hide a second layer of wool so warm that people harvest it as one of the rarest fibers in the world.

numbat.context_blurb: The numbat is a small, striped marsupial that lives in a few patches of eucalyptus woodland in Western Australia. It is one of the rarest mammals on the continent, and unlike almost every other Australian marsupial it is active during the day, trotting across the forest floor with a bushy tail held high. Numbats are specialists on a single colonial insect, and almost every feature of their body, from the shape of their mouth to their peg-like teeth, is built around that one meal.

okapi.context_blurb: The okapi is a shy forest mammal that lives in the dense Ituri rainforest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its back half is striped like a zebra and its front half is a rich chocolate color, but DNA puts it in a family with only one other living member, which it does not look much like at all. Okapis were unknown to Western science until the early 1900s, which is extraordinary for a mammal this size. They are solitary, use scent trails to communicate, and have a very long dark tongue they use for grooming and feeding.

pink-fairy-armadillo.context_blurb: The pink fairy armadillo is the smallest armadillo in the world, a palm-sized burrower that lives in the dry sandy grasslands of central Argentina. Its shell is pink and only loosely attached to its back, which has puzzled naturalists ever since the species was first described in 1825. It spends almost its entire life underground, swimming through loose sand with huge front claws, and is so rarely seen above the surface that scientists still know very little about how it lives.

proboscis-monkey.context_blurb: The proboscis monkey is a leaf-eating primate that lives only in the mangrove and riverine forests of Borneo. Males are famous for a huge, floppy nose that keeps getting bigger as they age, while females have a much smaller upturned one. The monkeys live in troops along slow rivers, swim well, and have unusual digestive machinery for a primate because of a tough, leaf-heavy diet. The male's exaggerated feature turns out to be a signal that females notice, which is why it keeps growing.

quokka.context_blurb: The quokka is a small, cat-sized marsupial from a few islands and patches of mainland Western Australia, best known for a face that looks like it is permanently smiling. It is a nocturnal grazer that climbs small trees and shelters in dense scrub during the heat of the day. Quokkas have become famous worldwide for a tourist phenomenon on Rottnest Island, where the lack of ground predators has left them unusually tame around people.

red-panda.context_blurb: The red panda is a small, cat-sized mammal with a rust-red coat and a long striped tail that lives in the cool bamboo forests of the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China. Despite the name, it is not closely related to the giant panda; DNA places it on its own branch of the tree of life, the only living member of its family. Red pandas spend almost all their time in trees, feed mostly on bamboo, and are now classified as endangered because of habitat loss.

saiga-antelope.context_blurb: The saiga antelope is a goat-sized grazing mammal of the central Asian steppes, stretching across Kazakhstan, Russia, Mongolia, and Uzbekistan. It survived from the ice age, when it ranged all the way from Britain to Alaska, and is now critically endangered. The saiga is famous for a huge, drooping nose that looks almost like a short trunk and completely dominates its face. Scientists study the saiga partly for that strange nose and partly because the whole species has been hit by sudden mass die-offs.

slow-loris.context_blurb: The slow loris is a nocturnal primate that lives in the rainforests of South and Southeast Asia. It is about the size of a small cat, moves slowly along branches with a hand-over-hand grip, and has huge eyes for seeing in the dark. The slow loris has one trick that makes it unique among primates and is one of a handful of mammals in the world capable of what it does. Illegal pet-trade videos have made it famous online, which is a serious problem because these animals do not do well in captivity.

solenodon.context_blurb: The solenodon is a shrew-like mammal the size of a large rat that lives on Hispaniola and Cuba in the Caribbean. It is a living fossil: its lineage branched off from other mammals before the dinosaurs went extinct, and it has barely changed since. Solenodons have long rubbery snouts, grooved teeth, and a trick in common with only a tiny number of other mammals. Introduced predators have pushed them to the brink of extinction, and most people have never heard of them.

tarsier.context_blurb: The tarsier is a tiny nocturnal primate from the islands of Southeast Asia, including the Philippines and Indonesia. It fits in a human palm but has enormous golden eyes, each one bigger than its own brain, and long finger-pad hands for gripping bamboo. Tarsiers are strict meat-eaters, which is unusual for a primate, and they hunt insects, small lizards, and even bats by making stunning leaps in near-total darkness. Their eyes and ears are tuned to signals humans cannot share.

tasmanian-devil.context_blurb: The Tasmanian devil is a dog-sized carnivorous marsupial that lives only on the island of Tasmania. It is squat, black, and loud: devils are famous for ear-splitting screams at feeding scuffles, which is how European settlers gave them their name. They are scavengers as much as hunters, with a jaw pound-for-pound among the strongest of any mammal. In the past 30 years, a transmissible facial cancer has pushed the species toward collapse, and biologists are watching closely to see whether they can adapt.

antlion-the-larva-that-digs-a-sand-death.context_blurb:
The antlion is a winged insect, but it is famous for its larva: a stubby, spiny little hunter that lives in loose, dry sand on every continent except Antarctica. The larva can spend two or three years in the sand, building a trap and letting gravity do most of its hunting for it.

In dry sand under a porch or along a path, the antlion larva scoops out a neat funnel and buries itself in the bottom, leaving just its jaws exposed, so an ant that touches the crumbling rim slides straight down into them.

If a victim scrambles halfway back up the wall, the larva jerks its head and showers it with flung sand, setting off little avalanches that carry the ant back down into its jaws. The larva can walk only backward, and as it wanders in reverse looking for a place to dig, it leaves squiggly trails in the sand, which is why North Americans call it the doodlebug.

A larva may sit in its pit for years and never leave a dropping, because it has no anus; all the waste from years of hunting stays stored inside its body until it becomes an adult. At last it spins a silk cocoon in the sand, and out comes an adult with long, delicate, lacewing-like wings, so unlike its larva that people often mistake it for a damselfly or a dragonfly, and it no longer eats ants.

assassin-bug-the-ambush-hunter-that-wear.context_blurb:
Assassin bugs are a huge family of long-legged, hook-beaked true bugs found across the warm parts of the world. They are ambush hunters that stalk other insects, and some species have invented ghoulish tricks, both for getting close to their prey and for hiding from their own enemies.

An assassin bug never chews: it stabs its victim with a curved beak, injects saliva loaded with paralyzing toxins and digestive enzymes that turn the insides to liquid, and then drinks that soup back up through the same beak, like sipping a milkshake through a straw. Its saliva can dissolve prey much larger than the bug itself.

The nymph of Acanthaspis petax drains ants dry and then cements the empty bodies into a heap on its back with sticky threads from special hairs on its belly, wearing a dozen or more of its victims as a disguise. In Australia, the feather-legged assassin bug takes on jack jumper ants larger than itself by offering bait: a gland coats a feathery hind leg with an intoxicating ooze, and when an ant grabs the leg to taste it, the bug twists around and drives its beak into the soft joint at the ant's neck. Entomologists call this the "fatal attraction" strategy.

To test whether the corpse backpack really works, the researchers Jackson and Pollard offered jumping spiders both bare nymphs and ant-covered ones, and the spiders attacked the bare nymphs about ten times as often, even when the bugs were dead and motionless, so the disguise itself fools the spider's eyes.

atlas-moth-one-of-the-biggest-moths-with.context_blurb:
The atlas moth of the tropical forests of South and Southeast Asia ranks among the biggest moths in the world. People who glimpse one often take it for a bird. Its adult life is short and single-minded, and the tips of its wings carry a famous warning to anything that tries to eat it.

Its wings span about 25 to 30 centimeters, nearly a foot across, and by surface area it carries more wing than almost any other insect.

The curved tip of each forewing is patterned like a cobra's head, and when a bird attacks, the moth flaps and writhes so the two "snake heads" rear up at the predator; its Cantonese name means "snake's head moth." An adult lives only a week or two, because its mouthparts are a tiny, useless stub: it can never eat, and it survives on fat it stored as a caterpillar, living only to mate and lay eggs.

The large female barely moves, clinging near her cocoon and releasing a scent into the night, while the smaller male flies in from kilometers away, tracking her with huge, feathery antennae that pick up her chemical signal.

bolas-spider-the-spider-that-fishes-with.context_blurb:
The bolas spider is a small, night-hunting spider of the Americas, Africa and Australasia. Unlike most spiders, the female spins no web to trap insects. She hunts a single kind of prey, moths, with a single strange tool, working more like a fisherman than a trap-builder.

Hanging from a branch in the dark, the female lets down a silk line tipped with a sticky glue ball and swings it at passing moths like a bolas, the weighted throwing cords of South American cowboys, which is how she got her name. By day she sits perfectly still on a little pad of silk spun over a leaf, her waxy-white, lumpy body looking exactly like a fresh bird dropping, so birds pass her by.

She does not wait for luck: she gives off a chemical that copies the scent a female moth releases to attract mates, so male moths follow the fake trail straight to her swinging glue ball.

One North American species, Mastophora hutchinsoni, fakes the scent of one moth species early in the evening, then switches to a second species' scent after 11 p.m., matching whichever moths are flying at that hour, so the catch on her glue ball changes as the night goes on.

The bullet ant is a large black ant of the lowland rainforests of Central and South America. It nests at the base of trees and sends its workers up into the canopy to forage. It is famous worldwide for one thing, its sting, which entomologists rank at the very top of the pain scale, and researchers keep returning to the chemistry of its venom.

The entomologist Justin Schmidt, who let insects sting him so he could rank their pain on a four-point scale, gave the bullet ant a perfect 4, and in The Sting of the Wild, his 2016 book, he compared the pain to walking across flaming charcoal with a three-inch nail driven into your heel.

The burning, throbbing waves of pain can go on for up to a full day, which is why people in Venezuela call it hormiga veinticuatro, the 24-hour ant. Among the Satere-Mawe of the Brazilian Amazon, a boy proves he is ready for manhood by wearing a woven glove of leaves packed with dozens of the live ants, stingers turned inward, for about ten minutes, enduring the pain in silence about twenty times over his youth. The ants are first calmed in an herbal solution and then woven into the glove.

The agony comes from poneratoxin, a small protein in the venom that jams the sodium channels nerves use to fire, scrambling their signals, yet no human death from the sting has been recorded, and the toxin clears the body within about a day.

diving-bell-spider-the-spider-that-lives.context_blurb: The diving bell spider is the only spider in the world that spends its entire adult life underwater. It lives in cool, slow ponds and weedy streams across Europe and parts of Asia. The spider hunts, mates, and raises its young beneath the surface, yet it still breathes air like any land spider; the puzzle of how it does that has fascinated naturalists since Victorian times. Its solution is elegant enough that engineers have borrowed the same name for a human diving device.

giant-weta-the-heavyweight-insect-of-new.context_blurb: The giant weta is a huge, flightless, cricket-like insect that lives only on a few small islands of New Zealand. Some of them are among the heaviest insects on Earth. Wetas are an ancient group, and they survived in New Zealand because the islands had no native land mammals, so they slowly took over the kinds of jobs mice and rats do in other ecosystems. They are now carefully protected, because introduced rats and stoats have pushed several species to the edge.

goliath-birdeater-the-biggest-spider-on-.context_blurb: The Goliath birdeater is the largest spider in the world by body mass, a dinner-plate-sized tarantula that lives in deep humid burrows of the Amazon rainforest in northern South America. Despite its name, it almost never eats birds; its usual prey are large insects, worms, and small frogs. The spider has urticating hairs on its abdomen that it flicks at threats, and it makes an audible hissing sound few other spiders can match. Biologists study it both for its size and for the limits of how big a spider can grow.

honeypot-ant-living-storage-jars-for-the.context_blurb: Honeypot ants are a group of ants that live in dry, hot places such as the deserts of Australia, Mexico, and the American Southwest. Food is rare and seasonal where they live, so the colony has evolved a strange and very specialized caste system in which some workers do almost nothing but store food on behalf of everyone else. These storage workers get so swollen they can barely move. Indigenous peoples of Australia have harvested honeypot ants as a traditional food for thousands of years.

jewel-wasp-the-wasp-that-turns-a-cockroa.context_blurb:
Shimmering metallic green and about 22 millimeters long, the emerald jewel wasp lives in tropical Africa and Asia. The female hunts cockroaches much bigger than herself, and what she does to them sounds like science fiction: she turns each victim into a living nursery for a single young wasp.

She does not kill her huge victim; she makes it an obedient zombie, alive but docile, that will later walk to its own grave.

Her first sting hits the nerve cluster that works the roach's front legs, paralyzing them for a couple of minutes, just long enough to hold the roach still while she aims a second, carefully placed sting. Afterward she grabs what is left of one antenna and leads the roach to her burrow like a dog on a leash, the roach walking on its own legs the whole way.

The second sting goes directly into the cockroach's brain, and the venom switches off its escape reflex: the roach can still walk, turn upright and even swim, but the drive to run from danger is gone. Neuroscientists study the venom because it blocks one behavior with surgical precision while leaving others intact. In the burrow she fixes one egg to the roach's side and closes the entrance. About three days later the egg hatches, and the larva chews a hole into the still-living roach, crawls inside and eats its organs from within, while the roach never fights back.

lord-howe-tree-lobster-the-stick-insect-.context_blurb: The Lord Howe tree lobster is a massive, dark-brown stick insect, big enough to fill a child's hand, that was thought extinct for more than 80 years after rats invaded its home island in the Pacific. Then biologists found a tiny population clinging to life in one specific place no rat could reach. The story of how it was rediscovered, bred in captivity, and prepared for release back to Lord Howe Island is one of the strangest comebacks in modern conservation.

new-zealand-glowworm-the-larva-that-fish.context_blurb: The New Zealand glowworm is not a worm at all but the larva of a small fly that lives inside damp caves and overhangs across New Zealand and parts of Australia. The larvae line cave ceilings with silk and hang long sticky threads below them, lit up by their own body chemistry. Tourists come from all over the world to see the ceilings covered in blue-green points of light. Scientists study the glowworm for both the chemistry of its light and the engineering of its silk.

ogre-faced-spider-the-net-caster-that-th.context_blurb: The ogre-faced spider, also called a net-casting spider, hunts at night in warm forests on several continents. Instead of waiting on a built web like most spiders, it holds a small, custom-made web stretched between its front legs and uses it as an active throwing net. It is named for a pair of enormous forward-facing eyes that give it one of the sharpest low-light visions of any arthropod. Scientists have recently shown that the spider can also detect prey without seeing them at all.

orchid-mantis-the-flower-that-eats-the-p.context_blurb: The orchid mantis is a small, pale pink or white praying mantis that lives in the rainforests of Southeast Asia. Its body is shaped and colored to look convincingly like a flower, down to petal-shaped flaps on its legs. For a long time naturalists assumed it was camouflaged for hiding, but careful fieldwork in the 2010s showed the whole setup is doing something more surprising than that, and biology textbooks have been rewriting the entry on it ever since.

tarantula-hawk-the-wasp-that-hunts-taran.context_blurb: The tarantula hawk is a very large, metallic-blue parasitoid wasp with rust-orange wings that is found in dry parts of the Americas, especially the American Southwest and Mexico. It hunts tarantulas, which are much bigger than it is, as food for its single offspring. The sting of a tarantula hawk is one of the most painful any insect can deliver, and the wasp has almost no natural predators because of it. Entomologists call it one of the clearest examples of an invertebrate specialist with no close rival.

trap-jaw-ant-jaws-that-snap-faster-than-.context_blurb: Trap-jaw ants are a group of ground-dwelling ants that live in warm forests around the world. Workers walk around with their mandibles cocked wide open like a mousetrap and then snap them shut on prey when sensory hairs are tripped. The speed of that snap puts the ant into the record books for one of the fastest motions ever measured in the animal kingdom. The ants also use the same mechanism in a surprising second way that has nothing to do with hunting.

treehopper-the-insect-with-alien-headgea.context_blurb: Treehoppers are small plant-sucking insects, related to cicadas, found in forests all over the world. They are famous among entomologists for a bizarre thing growing out of their backs: elaborate helmet-like shapes that can look like a thorn, an ant, a tiny mushroom, a wasp, or something out of a science-fiction comic. Scientists have argued for a century about how these helmets evolved and what they are really for. A single tropical forest can hold dozens of species, each with a different costume.

velvet-ant-the-cow-killer-that-is-really.context_blurb: The velvet ant, nicknamed the cow killer, is a brightly colored, fuzzy insect that walks across sunny ground in warm parts of North America. It is not actually an ant at all. The males have wings and look like typical wasps; the females are wingless and run across the ground, which is how the name got started. The velvet ant has one of the most painful stings of any insect in the United States, and it is also wrapped in several layers of defensive tricks on top of the sting.

velvet-worm-the-glue-cannon-hunter-of-th.context_blurb: Velvet worms are ancient, caterpillar-like animals that live in damp leaf litter in rainforests of the Southern Hemisphere, in places like South America, Australia, New Zealand, and southern Africa. They are not insects or worms; they are the only living members of their own branch of the tree of life, little changed from fossils more than 500 million years old. They are predators of small invertebrates, and they catch prey using a trick no other land animal has.

vinegaroon-the-whip-scorpion-that-sprays.context_blurb: The vinegaroon, also called a whip scorpion, is a nocturnal arachnid that lives in warm, dry regions from the American Southwest down into Mexico and parts of Asia. It looks like a scorpion crossed with a spider, with a long whip-like tail at the back instead of a stinger. Vinegaroons have no venom at all. Instead they defend themselves with a sharp-smelling chemical spray that scientists find useful partly because it comes out of the whip's base in a very precise, aimable jet.

zombie-ant-fungus-the-carpenter-ants-fat.context_blurb: The zombie-ant fungus is not actually an animal but a parasitic fungus of the genus Ophiocordyceps that infects carpenter ants in tropical rainforests, especially in Thailand and Brazil. The fungus takes over the ant's body in a very specific sequence of steps before killing it and bursting out to spread spores to the next victim. It is one of the most dramatic parasites known, and it has been featured in TV shows, video games, and medical research into fungal diseases.

armadillo-girdled-lizard-the-lizard-that.context_blurb:
The armadillo girdled lizard, Ouroborus cataphractus, is a small, armored lizard of the rocky deserts along South Africa's western coast. It hunts insects by day and shelters in cracks between the stones. Poaching for the pet trade has made it a protected species, and its armor and strange habits make it one of the most studied little reptiles of southern Africa.

Cornered by a mongoose on open rock, the lizard clamps its jaws onto its own tail and bends into a spiky loop, so its hard back and spined tail face outward on every side.

The point of the ring is its center, where the lizard tucks away its soft, unarmored belly, the one part a predator's teeth could pierce. Rows of thick, squarish, spiny scales cover its back and tail like a knight's suit of riveted plate armor, so teeth slide right off, and that armor plus the rolling-up trick explain why it is named after the armadillo. Unlike most lizards, it lays no eggs: after a pregnancy of six to eight months the female gives birth to live young, usually just one or two, and she is one of the few lizards that may care for her babies afterward.

It is also unusually social for a reptile, living in colonies of up to 30 to 60 lizards of all ages packed together in a single rock crevice. Most lizards live alone, so a crowded crack full of armored neighbors is a rare sight in the reptile world.

basilisk-the-lizard-that-runs-on-water.context_blurb:
The basilisk is a slim, bright-green, long-tailed lizard of the forest streams and rivers of Central and South America. When a predator surprises it near water, it pulls off one of the most famous escape tricks in nature. It eats both plants and small animals, lays its eggs on riverbanks, and can swim and dive if the trick fails.

Startled, it rears up on its hind legs and dashes across the surface of a stream without sinking, which looks so much like walking on water that people nicknamed it the Jesus Christ lizard, after the Bible scene of Jesus walking on the Sea of Galilee.

Water is always its escape route: a basilisk cornered on a branch will drop straight down from the tree into the stream below, then sprint or swim away and leave the land predator stranded.

Speed is everything, because its feet slap the water up to 20 times a second, so each foot is already lifting away before the water can close over it. Size matters too: a light young basilisk can sprint 10 to 20 meters across open water, but a heavy adult manages only a few meters before its weight breaks the surface and it sinks.

Could a person do the same? The biologists Glasheen and McMahon calculated that a human would have to slap the water faster than 30 meters per second, needing roughly 15 times the muscle power a person actually has, so no human ever will.

caecilian-the-legless-amphibian-whose-yo.context_blurb:
Caecilians are a little-known group of amphibians that burrow through warm, wet soil in the tropics of the Americas, Africa and Asia. They feed on worms and other small creatures, are rarely seen above ground, and look like nothing else in their class. Biologists have found one of their parenting habits especially startling: it sounds like a horror story, but it is really an act of care.

This legless, ringed, worm-shaped burrower is a caecilian, a true amphibian in the same class as frogs and salamanders, neither worm nor snake.

There are more than 220 species spread through the warm, wet tropics of several continents, but not one lives naturally in Australia. Nearly blind in the dark soil, it hunts with a chemical-sensing tentacle that sits in a groove between each eye and nostril and can be pushed out and pulled back, a sense organ unique among all vertebrates.

In the Kenyan caecilian Boulengerula taitanus, a mother's newly hatched young crawl over her and scrape at her with temporary hatchling teeth, peeling off and eating her fatty outer skin, which regrows in about three days, so they feed again and again and can gain up to ten times their weight in a week. Alexander Kupfer and his team first documented this skin-feeding, a form of maternal care, not cruelty.

Researchers in Brazil found in 2020 that Siphonops annulatus, the ringed caecilian, has tiny glands at the base of its teeth that release fluid carrying an enzyme also found in bee, wasp and snake venom, and if the finding is confirmed, caecilians may be the oldest land vertebrates with an oral venom system, older even than snakes. The finding is still under study.

darwins-frog-the-father-who-broods-young.context_blurb: Darwin's frog is a small, pointed-nosed frog that lives in the cool, mossy beech forests of southern Chile and Argentina. It was first described by Charles Darwin on his voyage of the Beagle in the 1830s and is now critically endangered. The frog is best known for an extraordinary parenting trick, in which the father does a job that in almost every other vertebrate is handled by the mother. Modern research is trying to figure out exactly how and when this strategy evolved.

draco-the-gliding-lizard-on-rib-wings.context_blurb: The Draco, also known as the flying dragon, is a small lizard that lives in the rainforest canopies of Southeast Asia and India. It spends most of its life clinging to tree trunks, where it is nearly invisible against the bark. When it needs to move between trees, it uses an anatomical trick that no other lizard has, flaring out a pair of wing-like flaps built from parts of its own skeleton. Draco cannot truly fly but can glide quite far between trunks without ever touching the ground.

flying-snake-the-serpent-that-glides.context_blurb: Flying snakes are a group of slender tree snakes that live in the forests of South and Southeast Asia. They do not have wings or any flap of extra skin, but they can glide long distances between trees anyway, steering with their bodies as they fall. Biologists at Virginia Tech have filmed them in slow motion to work out exactly how a snake with no limbs manages to turn gravity into a sideways jump. The snake is mildly venomous but harmless to humans; its real party trick is the glide.

gaboon-viper-the-longest-fangs-of-any-sn.context_blurb: The Gaboon viper is a thick, heavy snake that lives on the leaf-littered floors of African rainforests and woodlands. It is slow, patient, and almost invisible: the patterns on its back look exactly like dead leaves and dappled light. The Gaboon viper hunts by ambush and strikes with a weapon that puts it in a record book of its own among snakes. Despite its danger, it is a reclusive animal that rarely bites unless stepped on or handled.

hairy-frog-the-frog-that-breaks-its-own-.context_blurb: The hairy frog, also called the horror frog, is a stout frog from the rainforests of Central Africa. The nickname comes from thin skin filaments males grow during breeding season, which do a specific job tied to life in the fast streams where they live. The really strange thing about the hairy frog, though, is a defensive weapon it keeps hidden until a predator forces it out. Scientists first described the mechanism in the 1900s and have been studying it with X-rays and high-speed cameras ever since.

hellbender-the-giant-snot-otter-that-bre.context_blurb: The hellbender is a huge, flat-headed aquatic salamander that lives on the bottoms of cold, fast-flowing streams in the eastern United States. Adults can be nearly two feet long. The hellbender spends almost its entire life underwater, hiding beneath large flat rocks and ambushing crayfish, and it has a surprising answer to the problem of getting enough oxygen in cold water. The species is now in serious trouble because of pollution and the loss of the specific streambed shape it needs to lay eggs.

hognose-snake-the-drama-queen-death-fake.context_blurb: The eastern hognose snake is a stout, upturned-snout snake found across the eastern and central United States. It eats mostly toads and digs them out of sandy soil with its shovel-shaped nose. When threatened, the hognose puts on one of the most dramatic defensive shows of any animal in North America, moving through a whole sequence of bluffs before falling back on a last-ditch act. It is mildly venomous to its toad prey but harmless to humans; the real weapon is the performance.

leatherback-turtle-the-warm-blooded-rept.context_blurb: The leatherback sea turtle is the largest sea turtle on Earth, big enough that adults can weigh as much as a small car. Unlike other sea turtles, it has no hard shell: its back is a leathery hide stretched over a network of bony plates. Leatherbacks cross entire oceans between tropical nesting beaches and cold feeding grounds near the Arctic. They have a strange, mostly-jelly diet and a body-temperature strategy unusual for anything we normally call a reptile.

marine-iguana-the-only-sea-going-lizard.context_blurb: The marine iguana lives only on the Galapagos Islands and is the only lizard in the world that feeds in the sea. It is a stocky, dark-colored herbivore that dives into cold ocean water to graze on algae growing on submerged rocks. Marine iguanas are nothing like any mainland lizard; everything about them, from their snub-nosed heads to their flattened tails, has been reshaped by that one unusual meal. Charles Darwin, who famously called them imps of darkness, used them as evidence of how animals change over time.

mata-mata-turtle-the-leaf-that-vacuums-u.context_blurb: The mata mata is a strange, flat-headed turtle that lives on the leaf-covered bottom of slow-moving blackwater streams of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Its shell is heavily ridged and its neck is covered in fringes and tabs of skin that break up its outline. The mata mata is almost completely motionless by day, waiting for fish to come close. When one does, it uses an eating method that lets it swallow prey without ever opening its mouth around them in the normal way.

olm-the-blind-cave-baby-dragon-that-live.context_blurb:
Deep in the limestone caves of southeastern Europe, mostly in Slovenia, black underground rivers hide a pale, finger-sized salamander called the olm. It is blind, it never fully grows up, and it may live a hundred years, a life so slow that scientists study it for clues about aging.

For centuries, when floods in the caves washed olms up into the daylight, local people believed they were baby dragons, the young of a great beast sleeping deep beneath the earth.

The olm's pinkish skin is so like a person's in tone that it earned a second name. Slovene speakers call the olm the 'human fish.' It keeps a baby's body for life. Amphibians usually begin life as gilled larvae in the water and reshape their bodies as adults. The olm never makes that change, and even at a hundred it still wears the feathery external gills that an adult frog loses, a trait called neoteny that it shares with the axolotl.

Its eyes are tiny, sunk beneath the skin and useless in the pitch dark. Besides smell and hearing, the olm finds its tiny prey by sensing the weak electric fields their bodies produce, using special sense organs called ampullary organs.

Its whole life runs on almost no energy. It eats rarely, and when scientists tracked tagged olms for years, most had moved less than 10 meters. One was found in exactly the same spot after 2,569 days, more than seven years without going anywhere. As the researcher Gergely Balazs put it, they are "hanging around, doing almost nothing," a thrifty way to live for an animal that can last a century.

purple-frog-the-pig-nosed-frog-that-surf.context_blurb: The purple frog is a dark, bloated, pig-nosed frog that lives in the Western Ghats of India. It is one of the strangest frogs in the world, and it was only formally described by Western science in 2003. The frog spends almost its entire life hidden deep underground, feeding on termites, and surfaces for only a brief window each year to breed. Its evolutionary lineage splits off from almost every other living frog family and goes back to the age of the dinosaurs.

shingleback-skink-the-lizard-with-a-tail.context_blurb: The shingleback skink is a short, stocky Australian lizard with pine-cone-like scales. It is also called a sleepy lizard, bobtail, or stumpy. It lives in dry woodlands and grasslands across most of southern Australia and is usually seen basking on roadsides. The shingleback is unusual for a reptile in that it forms long-term monogamous pairs that return to each other every spring for many years. Its tail is also shaped and used in a specific way that fools a lot of predators.

spider-tailed-viper-the-tail-that-fishes.context_blurb: The spider-tailed horned viper is a small, dust-colored viper that lives in the rocky hills and ridges of western Iran. It is one of the most recently described venomous snakes, formally named in the 2000s, and biologists study it for a very specific hunting method it uses on migrating birds. The snake lies motionless among loose stones, waiting out the heat of the day, with only one tiny part of its body moving in a way that looks nothing like the rest of the snake at all.

surinam-toad-babies-that-erupt-from-the-.context_blurb: The Surinam toad is a flat, triangular, almost origami-shaped frog from the rivers and swamps of the Amazon basin. It is a lifelong swimmer and almost never leaves the water. Instead of a tongue, it uses sensitive fingertips to find prey in muddy water. The toad is best known among biologists for a reproductive strategy that is unlike anything else in the amphibian world and is the kind of thing people struggle to watch all the way through on video.

thorny-devil-drinking-through-skin-and-t.context_blurb: The thorny devil is a small, spiky lizard that lives in the dry deserts of central and western Australia. It is covered head to tail in sharp spines that make it look fierce, but the lizard is actually slow, harmless, and eats almost nothing except ants. The thorny devil's body is tuned around two very specific survival problems in the desert, and it has evolved separate, elegant solutions to each. Both solutions turn out to involve features that most people would never guess just from looking at it.

wallaces-flying-frog-the-frog-that-parac.context_blurb: Wallace's flying frog is a bright-green tree frog that lives in the rainforests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula. It was first described by the Victorian naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace during his years in the region in the 1850s. The frog spends almost all its time in the canopy, and when it needs to move between trees it does something no normal frog can do: it jumps and glides on a parachute built right into its own body.

why-the-ice-age-giants-died-overkill-vs-.context_blurb: At the end of the last ice age, between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most of the biggest land animals on every continent except Africa went extinct. Mammoths, giant sloths, saber-toothed cats, giant kangaroos, and many others disappeared in a wave that followed the arrival of modern humans and overlapped with sudden climate change. Scientists still argue about how much of the extinction was climate, how much was hunting pressure, and how much was both at once. The debate is one of the biggest in paleoecology.

archerfish.context_blurb:
The archerfish is a small, slim, silvery fish with bold black stripes, at home in mangrove creeks and brackish river mouths from Southeast Asia to northern Australia. It feeds on land insects perched far out of its reach, and it brings them down with one of the strangest weapons in the animal kingdom: water.

When a cricket, ant or spider sits on a leaf above the creek, the archerfish fires a precise jet of water from below the surface that knocks the insect off its perch and into the water, where the fish eats it.

Its aim is superb: an adult almost always hits on the very first shot, striking insects dead-on up to about 65 centimeters away, and its jet can reach prey as high as 3 meters.

The gun barrel is inside its mouth: the roof of its mouth has a deep channel, and the fish presses its tongue up against it, sealing the channel into a narrow tube, then snaps its gill covers shut to blast water through.

Water bends light at the surface, so from below a bug can appear as much as 25 degrees away from its real spot, yet the archerfish compensates for that bending and aims at the insect's real position. The fish's mouth muscles are too weak for such a hard hit, so the punch is built in flight: water fired last travels faster than water fired first, catching up and bunching the jet into one compact slug about six times more powerful than the muscles alone, the same physics an inkjet printer uses. Archerfish also learn by watching: in Stefan Schuster's 2006 study, fish that never fired during training matched the skill of the trained fish at hitting speeding targets as soon as they got a turn, having learned purely by observing the others.

box-jellyfish.context_blurb:
Box jellyfish live in warm coastal waters, especially off northern Australia and across the Indo-Pacific. They are pale and nearly invisible in the water, yet they swim with purpose, see with surprisingly complex eyes and carry one of the most dangerous stings of any animal on Earth, all without a brain.

The box jellyfish is named for its bell, a see-through cube with four flat sides instead of the rounded dome of an ordinary jellyfish, with a cluster of long tentacles trailing from each corner.

Unlike drifting jellyfish, it swims hard, squeezing its bell to jet along at about 1.5 meters per second, and it can whip around in a full 180-degree turn within a few pulses of its bell. Australia's deadliest box jellyfish, Chironex fleckeri, has 24 eyes, six apiece set in four tiny sensory clubs called rhopalia, yet it has no brain, only a ring of nerves around its bell.

Most of those eyes are simple patches that only sense light, but a few work like a camera, each with a lens, a cornea and a retina, able to form a picture, astonishing in an animal with no brain to make sense of it. Each tentacle carries hundreds of thousands of stinging capsules called nematocysts, tiny coiled harpoons that fire when they sense the chemicals on skin rather than at a mere bump, so they are not wasted on driftwood. Few animals carry deadlier venom than Chironex fleckeri: a serious sting can stop a person's heart, and untreated victims have died within two to five minutes, which is why swimmers on northern Australian beaches watch for it more carefully than for sharks.

Because the bell tumbles as it swims, each sensory club holds a heavy crystal called a statolith on a flexible stalk, and gravity pulls it straight down like a plumb bob, so the eyes stay pointed up and down no matter how the bell tilts.

coelacanth.context_blurb:
The coelacanth, Latimeria, is a large lobe-finned fish, deep blue in color, that lives in deep waters off eastern Africa and Indonesia. Its last fossils date to the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs, so scientists believed its whole group had vanished, until a live one turned up in 1938. It is closer kin to lungfish and to the ancestors of land animals than to a tuna or a trout.

In 1938 the young museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted a strange blue fish in a South African catch, with four thick, limb-like fins and a small extra tail, and it proved to be a coelacanth, the classic living fossil. J.L.B. Smith, the fish scientist who identified it, loved the fish so much that he titled his 1956 book Old Fourlegs, after its four leg-like fins.

Underwater film shows its four fleshy, muscle-tipped fins moving in the same alternating pattern a four-legged reptile uses when it walks, a hint of how life crawled onto land, though the coelacanth is not our direct ancestor. For sixty years that South African fish was the only kind known, until in 1997 the marine biologist Mark Erdmann, honeymooning in Indonesia with his wife Arnaz Mehta, spotted a second species laid out at a fish market in Sulawesi. It was later named Latimeria menadoensis.

Its skull has a true hinge running crosswise through the middle, something no other living animal has, and when it lunges, a special muscle swings the whole front of its head upward at that joint, opening its mouth extra wide and biting harder to swallow bigger prey. In 2021 scientists counted growth rings on coelacanth scales and found that a mother carries her young for about five years, the longest pregnancy of any animal known, before giving birth to 5 to 25 fully formed live pups. The same study found that coelacanths may live nearly a century and do not mature until about age 55.

cuttlefish.context_blurb: The cuttlefish is a short-bodied cephalopod related to octopuses and squid that lives in shallow seas around much of the world. It swims by rippling a long fin that runs down each side of its body. Cuttlefish are famous for their skin: in a fraction of a second they can turn themselves into a different pattern, texture, and color. They are also startlingly clever for an invertebrate, with large brains and complex visual tricks.

electric-eel.context_blurb: The electric eel is a long, dark fish of the slow, muddy rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Despite the name, it is not actually an eel but a kind of knifefish, more closely related to catfish. It is also one of only a handful of animals that can generate strong electric shocks, and it uses that electricity for many different jobs. Modern research has even shown it doing something no one expected a fish-shaped predator to do.

giant-and-colossal-squid.context_blurb: Giant and colossal squid are two different enormous deep-sea cephalopods that live far below the surface of the open ocean. Live sightings are extremely rare, and most of what scientists know about them comes from specimens recovered inside large predators that hunt them or washed up on remote beaches. Their eyes, their tentacles, and their life histories are all built for a world of near-total darkness and crushing pressure. The two species are not the same animal and have genuinely different body plans.

great-white-shark.context_blurb: The great white shark is a large, powerful shark that lives in cool and temperate oceans around the world, including the coasts of California, South Africa, Australia, and the Mediterranean. It can grow more than 20 feet long and is the biggest predatory fish alive today. Great whites hunt seals, sea lions, and other large marine prey using a mix of camouflage from below, bursts of speed, and senses tuned finely enough to pick up an injured animal at long range.

hammerhead-shark.context_blurb: The hammerhead shark is a group of shark species that live in warm oceans all over the world. They are named for the strange flattened, T-shaped extension of their heads, which is formally called a cephalofoil. The hammer is not a weapon in the usual sense; it is packed with sensors, and it changes how the shark hunts and swims. Some hammerhead species gather in enormous schools during the day in a few specific places, which is unusual for a predator this size.

horseshoe-crab.context_blurb: The horseshoe crab is a round, armored, almost helmet-shaped marine arthropod that lives in shallow water along the Atlantic coasts of North America and the Gulf and coasts of parts of Asia. It is not a true crab; it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions, and its lineage goes back more than 450 million years. Horseshoe crabs come ashore in huge spawning groups every spring. Modern medicine depends on them in a way most people never hear about.

mantis-shrimp.context_blurb: The mantis shrimp is a long, colorful marine crustacean that lives in warm shallow seas, mostly in burrows it digs in the sand. Despite the name, it is not a shrimp but belongs to its own ancient group called stomatopods. Mantis shrimp are famous for two things: a pair of hunting arms that strike with astonishing speed, and some of the most unusual eyes in the whole animal kingdom. Scientists keep updating what they think the shrimp can actually do with those eyes.

mudskipper.context_blurb:
When the tide drains out of tropical mangrove swamps and mudflats in Africa, Asia and parts of Australia, it leaves wide stretches of glistening mud. Most fish would be stranded. The mudskipper is just getting started: a bulgy-eyed fish that walks, leaps, fights and courts in the open air.

The mudskipper is a true fish, finger-length, yet it spends most of its life out of water, hauling itself over the mud instead of swimming.

To walk, it plants its two muscular pectoral fins like a pair of crutches and drags its body forward across the mud. When it needs speed, it changes gait. A sudden flex and push of its tail flings it through the air in a leap of up to about 61 centimeters, roughly two feet, and that skip is where the mudskipper gets its name.

Life in the air brings two problems: breathing and staying wet. Gills work poorly out of water. So, like a frog, the mudskipper absorbs air through its damp skin and through the moist lining inside its mouth and throat. Before a long trek across the mud, it fills its enlarged gill chambers with a mouthful of water and air, puffing out its cheeks like a scuba diver's tank, because if its gills dry out it can no longer take in oxygen. A male defends his patch of mud with a wild show: he rears up in push-ups, flares the fin on his back, beats his tail and leaps high. The display does double duty, warning rival males away while also showing off to impress females.

A mudskipper father's real masterpiece is underground. In tropical Asia, a male hollows out a burrow whose arched roof holds a pocket of air, then makes trip after trip to the surface to gulp air and carry it down; the biologist Karen Martin found that he may need about 100 mouthfuls to build that first air bubble for his eggs. For days he keeps the chamber stocked while he watches the tide. When the moment is right, he swallows the trapped air out of the chamber and lets the rising sea pour in, so the eggs can hatch and the larvae swim off to sea. Martin called him "really a very good papa."

nautilus.context_blurb: The nautilus is a deep-sea cephalopod from the warm waters of the western Pacific. Unlike octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, it has kept the external shell that its ancestors wore for hundreds of millions of years. The shell is a beautiful coiled spiral divided into gas-filled chambers, which lets the nautilus float and sink without burning energy. Nautilus bodies also keep features that other cephalopods have lost, which is why biologists keep returning to it as a window into cephalopod history.

ocean-sunfish-mola.context_blurb: The ocean sunfish, also called the mola, is a huge, round, nearly tailless fish of the open ocean. Adults can weigh over a ton, which makes them the heaviest bony fish in the world. They drift on their sides at the surface, dive deep after jellyfish, and are often covered in parasites they clean off in a strange social arrangement with other animals. Despite their size, molas start life as microscopic larvae that are nothing like the adults, and the transformation between the two stages is one of the biggest size jumps in all of vertebrate biology.

octopus.context_blurb: The octopus is a soft-bodied cephalopod found in every ocean on Earth, from tide pools to the deep sea. It has eight arms covered in sensitive, grippy suckers, three hearts, and a nervous system split between a central brain and the arms themselves. Octopuses solve problems, open jars, remember individual humans, and change their skin in ways that make them one of the clearest cases of intelligence outside of vertebrates. Scientists study them to understand how a mind so different from ours can work at all.

pistol-shrimp.context_blurb: The pistol shrimp is a small marine crustacean that lives in warm, shallow seas around the world. It has one normal pincer and one enormous one, and it uses the big one as a weapon in a way that would be hard to believe without high-speed video. Pistol shrimp also share burrows with gobies in one of the ocean's clearest examples of two unrelated species living together to each other's benefit.

portuguese-man-o-war.context_blurb: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish but is actually something much stranger: an entire colony of specialized animals that live and work together as one unit. It drifts on the surface of warm ocean currents, especially the Atlantic and Pacific trade-wind zones, under a glassy, blue-tinted gas-filled float. Beneath the float trail long stinging tentacles that paralyze fish. The sting is painful to humans but almost never fatal; the man o' war's real trick is a kind of cooperation most animals cannot pull off.

sea-cucumber.context_blurb: The sea cucumber is a sausage-shaped marine invertebrate that lives on the sea floor in every ocean, from shallow reefs down into the deep abyss. Despite its soft, slow look, it is an echinoderm, a cousin of sea stars and sea urchins. The sea cucumber feeds by vacuuming up sand or filtering water, and when threatened it has a bizarre and genuinely weird defensive move that most people, on seeing it the first time, have trouble believing is real.

sea-star.context_blurb: The sea star, sometimes called the starfish, is a radially symmetric marine animal that lives in oceans worldwide, from shallow tide pools to the deep sea. It is not a fish at all; it is an echinoderm, a cousin of sea urchins, sand dollars, and sea cucumbers. Sea stars have no brain and no blood in the usual sense. They move, feed, and heal using a surprising hydraulic system under their skin and a few other tricks that biologists have been peeling apart for over a hundred years.

seahorse.context_blurb: The seahorse is a small, upright-swimming fish that lives in shallow, warm, seagrass-filled waters around much of the world. It has a horse-shaped head, a prehensile tail that grips weeds like a monkey's, and a cluster of body-plan features that make it one of the strangest fish on Earth. Everything about the seahorse is slow and precise, from how it feeds to how it reproduces. The male and female of a pair tend to stay together for a long time.

whale-shark.context_blurb: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the ocean, a slow, spotted shark that can grow more than 40 feet long. It lives in warm seas around the world and is a specialist on some of the smallest food in the sea. Whale sharks gather in a few predictable places each year, which is where researchers and tourists go to see them. The entire body of this huge animal is built around that one specialized meal, and biologists are still learning where they go when they leave the known gathering sites.

beaver.context_blurb:
The beaver, a hefty rodent with a paddle of a tail, lives along the streams and rivers of North America and Eurasia. Few animals reshape their world as it does: it fells trees, dams streams into ponds and turns ponds into wet meadows. Its waterproof fur, scaly tail and strange teeth all serve that life between land and water.

Its front teeth are bright orange, because the outer enamel is packed with iron instead of the magnesium found in most animal teeth, which makes them harder and more resistant to acid and decay. Those teeth keep growing for life: new tooth forms at the root as fast as the tip wears away, so even an old beaver has a working set and must gnaw constantly. Its home, a dome of mud and sticks called a lodge, has its entrance underwater, so a beaver family gets in by diving while a fox or wolf on the bank cannot follow. The dam floods a safe moat all around the home.

The iron-hard enamel coats only the front face of each incisor, while the softer dentin behind it wears away faster, so every bite grinds the tooth back into a sharp chisel edge and the teeth sharpen themselves. Underwater a beaver keeps its eyes open behind a see-through third eyelid that slides across each eye like built-in swim goggles. Its broad, flat, scaly tail is a rudder for steering, and when danger appears, the beaver slaps it hard on the water with a loud crack that warns the whole colony.

In autumn it stocks an underwater larder of branches for winter, and before diving with a branch in its teeth it seals itself shut: valve-like muscles close its nostrils and ears, and its lips seal behind the jutting front teeth, so it can carry wood underwater for up to about 15 minutes without swallowing water.

Beavers also build big: in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, generations of beaver families raised a dam about 800 meters long, as long as eight football fields, and in 2007 the researcher Jean Thie spotted it in satellite images. It is the largest beaver dam known, and today conservationists use beavers as ecosystem engineers to restore damaged land.

camel.context_blurb:
The camel is a long-legged desert mammal of North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. People have ridden and loaded camels for thousands of years, but the animal's own biology is the real marvel. Nearly every part of its body solves a single problem: staying alive where water is scarce and the heat is fierce.

The one-humped dromedary is the hot-desert specialist, while the Bactrian camel, with two humps and a thick coat, belongs to the cold Gobi of Central Asia, where a single year swings from roughly -20°F to 120°F. On loose sand, each broad, two-toed foot spreads and flattens under the camel's weight and then pulls in as it lifts, working like a snowshoe that keeps it from sinking where a horse's narrow hooves would bog down.

Contrary to popular belief, the hump holds no water: it is a concentrated store of fat that the camel burns when food runs short, which is why a hungry camel's hump shrinks and flops to one side. Packing the fat into one hump, rather than under all its skin, also helps the rest of the body shed heat. A camel can even chew up a spiny cactus, because cone-shaped bumps of keratin lining its mouth turn the needles so they slide down its throat point-first. A vet described those bumps as feeling almost like plastic.

A badly dehydrated camel can drink well over 100 liters in about ten minutes, up to 145 liters at one go by the San Diego Zoo's count, replacing about a third of its body weight almost at once. Instead of sweating away precious water, a camel lets its body temperature swing, cooling to about 34 to 35°C overnight and climbing to 41 or 42°C by day, storing the heat in its body rather than spending water to shed it.

cheetah.context_blurb:
On the dry grasslands of Africa, with a last small population in Iran, lives a slender spotted cat built for one thing: the sprint. The cheetah lacks the bulk other big cats use to wrestle prey or climb, and nearly every part of it, inside and out, serves the chase.

No land animal is faster than the cheetah: from a standstill it can top 110 kilometers an hour, about 70 miles an hour, barely three seconds later, out-accelerating many sports cars. Small black spots cover its golden coat, and the pattern they make, together with the rings on its tail, is unique to each cheetah, like a human fingerprint, so researchers can tell individuals apart from photographs.

A cheetah cannot roar. It purrs, growls, hisses and stutters. A mother calling her cubs out of the tall grass uses a high, birdlike chirp. Other cats keep sharp claws tucked away until they strike, but a cheetah's claws are blunt and only partly retractable, poking out like a dog's so they dig into the dirt with every stride, the way spikes grip on a sprinter's shoes. Ridged paw pads add grip like tire tread.

The black 'tear marks' running from the inside of each eye down to the mouth soak up the sun's glare off its cheeks, like an athlete's eye-black, so it can keep prey in sharp focus on the bright plains. Its unusually flexible spine coils and springs open with every bound, flinging its hind feet out ahead of its front ones. At full gallop it is airborne twice per stride, once stretched out and once bunched up. When a gazelle jinks sideways, the cheetah swings its long tail as a counterweight to shift its balance, with the flattened, ringed tip working as a rudder, so it can take hairpin turns that would send other animals tumbling.

All that speed has a price. A sprint devours oxygen, so the cheetah gulps air through enlarged nostrils that open into roomy, air-filled sinuses, its breathing leaping from about 60 breaths a minute to around 150, fed by an oversized heart and lungs. Even so, top speed lasts only seconds. Its muscles burn fuel faster than oxygen arrives, lactic acid floods them, and the cat runs out of energy, which is why it must catch its prey within about 30 seconds or give up.

When five wild Botswana cheetahs wore GPS-and-motion collars, they did hit 93 kilometers an hour, but most hunts were run at a moderate pace and won by footwork: a firm grip, sharp maneuvering, and the muscle power to brake hard and turn. During the ice age, North America was home to a lean, spotted sprinter called Miracinonyx, long counted as an 'American cheetah.' Genetic and skeletal studies showed it was really a close relative of the cougar that evolved the same fast-chasing body independently, a textbook case of convergent evolution. In 1985 Stephen O'Brien's team grafted skin between fourteen unrelated cheetahs. A graft between unrelated lions is rejected as foreign, yet all fourteen healed in, as if they had passed between identical twins. A severe population bottleneck in the species' recent past left cheetahs so nearly identical at the genes the immune system uses to tell self from stranger that one cat's skin reads to another as its own. Wild-born cheetahs are just as uniform, so zoo breeding is not the cause.

echidna.context_blurb: The echidna is a short, spiny mammal that lives in Australia and New Guinea. Along with the platypus, it is one of the only two living kinds of mammal that still lays eggs, a trait kept from a lineage older than the dinosaurs. Echidnas live mostly solitary lives, dig for ants and termites, and have a snout packed with sensors that would be impressive on any animal. They also do some things related to reproduction and temperature control that remind biologists how strange their family tree is.

elephant.context_blurb: The elephant is the largest land animal on Earth. There are three living species: the African savanna, the African forest, and the Asian elephant. All three live in close family groups led by an older female, and all three have the same long, muscular, boneless trunk, which is one of the most capable grasping organs in the animal kingdom. Elephants are famously intelligent and emotionally complex. Biologists study them for their communication, their memory, and their long slow life histories.

giraffe.context_blurb: The giraffe is the tallest living land animal, a long-legged, long-necked ruminant of the savannas and woodlands of Africa. Adults can be nearly 18 feet tall. Giraffes feed in the tops of acacia trees, live in loose herds with no permanent leader, and have a prehensile tongue they use to pluck leaves around thorns. Their heart, blood pressure, legs, and neck are all engineered for the problem of being that tall, and they do several things related to that problem no other mammal does.

gray-wolf.context_blurb:
The gray wolf is the largest wild member of the dog family, a hunter of forests, tundra and mountains across the northern half of the world. Wolves live and hunt as a team, run down prey bigger than themselves, and, as Yellowstone National Park has shown, can reshape a whole landscape.

A wolf pack is a family: a mother and father, the breeding pair, with the young they have raised over the last few years. A family spread over a huge territory needs a long-range voice. On the open Arctic tundra, with no trees to muffle it, one wolf's howl carries about 10 miles; in forest, about 6.

Wolves howl to gather the pack before and after a hunt, to find each other when a storm scatters them, and to warn neighboring packs off their territory. They hunt by endurance rather than speed; a fit deer wins a short dash. Trotting at about 5 miles an hour for hours, a wolf tracking prey can cover more than 50 miles in a day, and one was seen chasing a deer for 12 miles.

Seven or eight wolves facing a hundred elk cannot just charge in. Instead the pack works to cut one animal away from the group, testing many, since most hunts of big hoofed prey fail; an elk that stands its ground is often left alone, while one that runs or seems weak becomes the target. For decades people pictured an 'alpha wolf' that fought its way to the top. L. David Mech, the biologist whose 1970 book spread that idea, corrected himself in 1999: the alpha picture came from captive strangers thrown together, and in a wild pack the wolves the others follow are just the parents. The whole pack helps raise the pups: babysitters guard the den, and when the hunters return, the pups lick at their mouths and the adults regurgitate meat they swallowed at the kill for pups too small for raw meat.

When gray wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 after about 70 years away, elk stopped lingering in the exposed valleys along the streams, and the willow and aspen they had chewed down began to grow tall again. Taller willows brought beavers back to build dams, a chain scientists call a trophic cascade. Researchers caution that the effect, though real, is sometimes overstated, since drought, bears and human hunters also thinned the elk.

hippopotamus.context_blurb:
The hippopotamus is a barrel-shaped giant of three tons or more that wallows in African waters from the Nile to the Zambezi. Its name means 'river horse,' but it is no horse. It spends its days in the water and comes out at dusk to graze.

The hippopotamus eats nothing but grass, yet it kills an estimated 500 or more people in Africa each year, more than lions or sharks do. It does not hunt people; its danger lies in its temper and its sheer bulk.

A hippo is too dense to float, so it cannot really swim; to cross deep water it strides along the river floor, kicking off the bed in a slow-motion underwater gallop with its toes barely touching down.

Scientists once grouped the hippo with pigs because of its molars, but blood-protein and DNA evidence showed that its closest living relatives are the whales and dolphins. The two lines probably split from a shared, water-loving ancestor about 55 million years ago. When a hippo flings its mouth open almost flat, nearly 150 degrees from jaw to jaw, it is not yawning but warning a rival. The gape shows off its real weapons: tusk-shaped canine teeth that keep growing all its life, reaching about 50 centimeters, kept sharp by grinding against the lower incisors.
