honey-badger.context_blurb: The honey badger is a stocky, low-slung carnivore that lives across much of Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. It is only distantly related to true badgers; it is more like an oversized weasel. The honey badger has a reputation as one of the toughest small predators on Earth. It will take on cobras, porcupines, and even young lions, and it tends to win in ways that have made it a favorite animal of wildlife documentaries. Its skin and chemistry help explain how it gets away with it.

kangaroo.context_blurb: The kangaroo is a group of large marsupials that live in Australia, where they are the dominant native grazer. The biggest, the red kangaroo, can top six feet standing up. Kangaroos travel using one of the most efficient movement systems any big animal has ever evolved, and they also do things related to reproduction and group life that no placental mammal matches. They are now so numerous in parts of the Australian outback that they are managed as both an icon and a problem.

koala.context_blurb: The koala is a small, grey, pouched tree-climbing marsupial that lives in the eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia. It is one of the pickiest eaters in the mammal world, surviving almost entirely on a single kind of plant that is tough, oily, and mildly poisonous. Koalas spend most of the day asleep because that diet gives so little energy. The animal is a specialist in every sense, from its gut to its paws to the slow rhythm of its day, and it is now listed as endangered in some Australian states after years of habitat loss and fire.

naked-mole-rat.context_blurb: The naked mole-rat is a small, pink, nearly hairless rodent that lives in long underground tunnels in the dry grasslands of East Africa. It looks almost like a wrinkled little sausage with teeth. The naked mole-rat is extraordinary among mammals for its social life, which is organized more like a bee colony than like a rodent nest. It is also extraordinary for how long it lives, how little it ages, and how it handles conditions that would kill almost any other mammal. Biomedical researchers study it closely for exactly these reasons.

pangolin.context_blurb: The pangolin is a scale-covered mammal that lives in Africa and across much of South and Southeast Asia. It is sometimes called a scaly anteater, but it is not closely related to anteaters at all; it belongs to its own order of mammals. Pangolins eat almost nothing except ants and termites, which they lap up with a tongue that is extraordinary even by the standards of ant-eaters. They are now the most trafficked mammal in the world because of demand for their scales, and every living species is at serious risk.

platypus.context_blurb: The platypus is a small, duck-billed, beaver-tailed mammal that lives in the freshwater streams and rivers of eastern Australia. When the first platypus specimen reached European naturalists in 1799, many assumed it was a fake. The platypus is a monotreme, one of only two mammal groups still laying eggs, and it has an unusually long list of features that no other living mammal shares. It swims with its eyes shut, finds prey with senses other mammals do not have, and the males carry a weapon unique among furred animals.

polar-bear.context_blurb:
The polar bear lives on the frozen sea of the Arctic, from Alaska and northern Canada through Greenland to the Russian coast. Its scientific name, Ursus maritimus, means 'sea bear,' and it earns it, hunting seals from the ice and swimming between floes. Almost everything about its body is built for cold.

The polar bear is the biggest bear alive and the heaviest meat-eater on land: a big male can weigh up to 800 kilograms, about 1,760 pounds, and rise nearly ten feet tall on his hind legs. Its signature hunting method takes patience, not speed. In still-hunting, the bear finds a seal's breathing hole in the ice and waits beside it without moving, sometimes for an hour or more, ready to strike the moment a seal comes up for air.

Its front paws measure up to 30 centimeters, a full foot, across, and like snowshoes they spread the bear's weight so it pads over soft snow without sinking; in the water they double as paddles. Under that famous coat is a surprise. A polar bear's skin is jet black, showing only on its nose and footpads, and the dark skin soaks up the sun's warmth like a solar panel. That black nose is a formidable tool. A polar bear can smell a seal's breathing hole about a mile away, and can sniff out a seal hidden under three feet of packed snow.

Even the white is an illusion. Each hair is clear, with a hollow, air-filled core, and the fur only looks white because the rough, hollow hairs scatter sunlight, just as snow does. With dense underfur and thick blubber beneath, that coat keeps the bear's body near 99°F at forty below. The fur, underfur and blubber hold its heat in so well that the bear's outer surface stays almost as cold as the snow, so on an infrared camera the huge animal nearly vanishes.

As the summer ice thins, a polar bear may have to cross long stretches of open water. In one tracking study, a female wearing a GPS collar in Alaska's Beaufort Sea swam about 426 miles without once hauling out, a nonstop swim of nine days, and lost 22 percent of her body weight before she reached solid ice.

sloth.context_blurb: The sloth is a group of slow-moving, long-clawed mammals that live upside down in the rainforest canopies of Central and South America. There are two living families, three-toed and two-toed, and both move more slowly than almost any other mammal. Sloths descend to the ground only every week or so and do almost everything, including eat, sleep, and give birth, hanging from branches. Their slowness is a strategy, not an accident, and it drives several surprising ecological relationships.

star-nosed-mole.context_blurb: The star-nosed mole is a small, nearly blind, insect-eating mammal that lives in the wet soils and shallow ponds of the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. The animal is best known for the strange, 22-fingered pink rosette on the tip of its snout. The star is not an olfactory organ; it is a touch organ, and it operates at a speed that puts the star-nosed mole into the record books among mammals. Scientists study it closely for what it says about how brains handle rapid sensory information.

vampire-bat.context_blurb: The vampire bat is a small bat that feeds entirely on the blood of other animals. There are three living species, all in Central and South America. The vampire bat is extraordinary in several ways: it can run on the ground almost like a four-legged animal, it shares food with roost-mates that are starving, and it has a specific set of body features for its very specialized meal. Scientists have also learned surprising things from vampire bats about how memory, friendship, and reciprocity work in a non-primate brain.

wolverine.context_blurb: The wolverine is a stocky, bear-like mammal that lives in the boreal forests and mountain tundras of the far north, across Scandinavia, Russia, Canada, and Alaska. It is one of the most powerful carnivores for its size on Earth and can drive even wolves and bears off a kill. Wolverines range over huge territories, cache food in the snow for lean times, and are built around life in deep cold. They are rare, hard to find, and remain one of the least-studied large carnivores in North America.

barreleye-macropinna-microstoma.context_blurb:
The barreleye, Macropinna microstoma, is a small deep-sea fish of the open Pacific that hovers some 600 to 800 meters below the surface, where the last sunlight dims to almost nothing. For decades scientists knew it only from damaged bodies hauled up in nets. Then robot submarines from California's Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, or MBARI, filmed it alive and revealed one of the strangest heads in the sea.

Only about 15 centimeters long, the barreleye wears a transparent, fluid-filled dome over the top of its head, so you can look right through it. Inside the dome sit its real eyes, two glowing green tubes that rest pointing straight up through the clear skull, watching for prey silhouetted against the faint light drifting down from above.

The two dark spots on the front of its face, right where eyes ought to be, are not eyes at all but nostrils, its organs of smell, and they fooled the first people to see one. For decades scientists wondered how a fish that only looks up could guide food into its tiny mouth, until MBARI showed in 2008 that the tubular eyes can rotate forward inside the dome, swiveling like binoculars to follow prey down to the mouth.

The scientists Robison and Reisenbichler saw that the eyes swing forward as the fish tips its whole body from horizontal to vertical to feed, so the eye turn is tied to the body's roll rather than happening on its own. The barreleye barely swims, holding its place almost perfectly still with large, flat fins that make tiny, precise adjustments.

It is thought to steal from siphonophores, drifting colonies whose stinging tentacles stretch beyond 10 meters, plucking small animals already snared there, and its see-through dome probably protects its delicate eyes from the stinging cells. Captured barreleyes have had jelly fragments in their stomachs. The fish was named in 1939 by W. M. Chapman, but every specimen came up in a net with its fragile dome collapsed or torn away, so drawings left it out until MBARI filmed a living barreleye with its dome intact in 2004, 65 years later.

blobfish-psychrolutes-marcidus.context_blurb:
The blobfish, Psychrolutes marcidus, lives on the deep seabed about a kilometer down off Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand. It became famous online as the world's saddest fish, thanks to photos of a droopy pink blob on a boat deck. Those photos show what happens when the fish leaves home, not what it really looks like.

Down in the deep it looks like an ordinary fish, blunt-headed and pink, with big black eyes and feathery fins, its jelly-soft body held in shape by the weight of the water above.

At home the water presses on it 60 to 120 times harder than air presses on us, and its body is built to work against that squeeze, so when a trawl hauls it to the surface and the pressure disappears, the body sags and collapses like a washed-up jellyfish. Its body is mostly jelly, with almost no muscle and very little bone, because chasing prey would waste energy that is scarce in the hungry deep, so it hovers almost motionless and gulps small crustaceans, sea snails and drifting scraps that pass right in front of its mouth. As one expert put it, being lazy is a survival strategy.

The famous photo shows a museum specimen nicknamed Mr Blobby, netted in 2003 on the Norfolk Ridge northwest of New Zealand, and the alcohol used to preserve him tightened his skin and shrank his nose, making his droopy face look even sadder. In 2013 a British comedy group's poll crowned the blobfish the ugliest animal in the world.

deep-sea-anglerfish-ceratioidei.context_blurb: The deep-sea anglerfish is a group of several hundred species that live in the dark middle and lower layers of the world's oceans, far below the surface. The females are large, ugly ambush predators with a glowing lure that dangles over their mouths. The males are tiny by comparison and lead a very different kind of life. Reproduction in deep-sea anglerfish is one of the strangest arrangements in the vertebrate world and has been giving biology textbooks a reliable showpiece for over a century.

electric-catfish-malapteruridae.context_blurb: The electric catfish is a family of large freshwater catfish that live in slow, muddy rivers across much of tropical Africa, including the Nile. They are strong, nocturnal predators with soft, scaleless skin. Electric catfish are one of only a handful of fish groups that generate their own strong electrical shocks, and the people of ancient Egypt knew them long before any modern biologist did. Modern research is still mapping out exactly how the catfish's body produces and controls those shocks.

elephantnose-fish-gnathonemus-petersii.context_blurb:
A small, dark fish of the slow, muddy rivers of West and Central Africa, the elephantnose hunts at night in water too murky for eyes to help, and it carries one of the biggest brains, for its size, of any fish. Nearly all of that brain serves one remarkable sense.

An organ near its tail gives off a weak electric field, and receptors all over its skin feel how nearby objects bend that field, letting the fish 'see' shape and distance in total darkness. Biologists call this active electrolocation.

The fish is named for the long, bendy flap that hangs from its face like an elephant's trunk, but the flap is no nose; its real nostrils are tiny and sit farther up. The 'trunk' is a movable extension of its chin, the schnauzenorgan, which the fish sweeps over the riverbed like a metal detector, feeling for buried insect larvae.

The electric sense can even tell the living from the dead. A larva and a pebble of the same size may lie side by side in the mud, and the fish knows which is which without seeing either. Living tissue stores electric charge like a tiny capacitor, while stone and mud only resist the current, and the fish feels that difference.

This sense is called electroreception, and it is costly: the brain that runs it burns about 60 percent of the fish's oxygen, roughly three times the share of any other backboned animal measured. It pays off in company. In a group, each fish can also read the pulses its neighbors give off, so the school works like a shared radar network and each member senses about three times farther than it could alone.

flashlight-fish-anomalopidae.context_blurb: The flashlight fish is a small, dark reef fish that lives in warm tropical oceans around the world and is best known in the Caribbean, the Indo-Pacific, and the Red Sea. The fish spends the day in deep water or inside caves and comes out at night to feed. It is named for a pair of large patches of glowing tissue on its face, which it can switch on and off like a car headlight. The light does several jobs for the fish, and researchers have carefully worked out what each of them is.

frogfish-antennariidae.context_blurb:
The frogfish is a small, lumpy, almost round fish of warm reefs around the world, and one of the sea's great masters of disguise. Matched in color and texture to the sponges, corals and seaweed around it, it can sit in plain view while divers swim past. It never chases a meal; it makes the meal come to it.

A frogfish hardly swims at all; it walks across the reef floor, setting down its stubby, limb-like fins one after another like feet. Its hunting gear grows from its head: the first spine of its back fin has become a thin fishing rod tipped with a fleshy bait shaped like a worm, shrimp or tiny fish, and the frogfish wiggles it until curious small fish swim close.

If a quick fish bites the bait clean off, the frogfish simply grows a new lure over about four to six months. When prey comes within reach, the strike takes about six milliseconds, some fifty times faster than the blink of an eye, which lasts around 300 milliseconds; no fish has been measured striking faster.

The strike is a vacuum, not a bite: the floor of the mouth drops and the cavity swells to as much as twelve times its resting volume, and the sudden space sucks the prey in with a rush of water. With no teeth to cut its food, the frogfish swallows everything whole, and its stomach stretches enough to take a fish as large as itself, or larger.

One species breaks even the frogfish rules: the psychedelic frogfish, found off Indonesia in 2008 and swirled with wild colors, pushes off with its fins and jets water from its gills, bouncing across the seabed like a rubber ball with its tail curled to one side.

gulper-eel-pelican-eel-eurypharynx-pelec.context_blurb: The gulper eel, also called the pelican eel, is a slender deep-sea fish that lives at depths of about one to two miles down in the open ocean. It has a tiny head, a huge expandable mouth, a stretchy stomach, and a long whip-like tail. Live gulper eels are almost never seen; most specimens come from trawl nets. In 2018, a video from a submersible caught one doing something unexpected, which quickly went viral in scientific circles.

handfish-brachionichthyidae.context_blurb: Handfish are a group of extremely rare, hand-sized fish that live only in a few patches of sea bottom around Tasmania. Instead of swimming, they walk across the sand on fins that look remarkably like little hands. There are several species, and some are among the most endangered fish in the world. Everything about the handfish, from its movement to its tiny range to its unusual eggs, is of close interest to Australian marine biologists.

hatchetfish-sternoptychidae.context_blurb: The hatchetfish is a small, flat-sided deep-sea fish shaped like the blade of a hatchet. It lives in the upper mesopelagic zone, several hundred meters down in oceans around the world. Hatchetfish are silvery, mirror-sided fish with huge upward-facing eyes and a line of light-producing organs along their undersides. That light is used in a specific survival trick that is one of the clearest examples of how a fish can hide in open water that has nowhere to hide at all.

leafy-sea-dragon-phycodurus-eques.context_blurb: The leafy sea dragon is a close relative of the seahorse that lives only off the southern coast of Australia. It is covered in long, leaf-shaped flaps of skin that blend in perfectly with the swaying kelp forests where it lives. The sea dragon is a slow, drifting predator on tiny crustaceans, and it does not swim with any of the usual power. Breeding sea dragons also share some of the strange reproductive habits of their seahorse cousins.

oarfish-regalecus-glesne.context_blurb: The oarfish is a long, silvery, ribbon-shaped fish that lives in the open ocean a few hundred meters below the surface. It can grow more than 20 feet long, which may make it the longest bony fish in the world. Oarfish are almost never seen alive; most known specimens are animals that washed up on beaches or came up sick. Their shape, size, and bright-red fins have fueled a very long history of sea-serpent stories around the world.

sarcastic-fringehead-neoclinus-blanchard.context_blurb: The sarcastic fringehead is a small, bad-tempered fish of the shallow coastal waters off California and Baja California. It is a territorial ambush hunter that lives inside empty shells, bottles, and crevices on the sea floor. The fringehead is best known among divers for an aggressive display it uses against rivals, which involves part of its own anatomy doing something no fish would be expected to do. Its face has gone viral in underwater photography more than once.

sheepshead-fish-archosargus-probatocepha.context_blurb: The sheepshead is a striped, panfish-sized fish of the shallow Atlantic coast of North America, from New York down into the Gulf of Mexico. It is a popular target for anglers in Florida and the Carolinas. The sheepshead lives mostly around rocks, pilings, and oyster beds, and it has an unusual set of teeth for a fish, teeth that look so much like a human mouth that photos of them regularly surprise people on the internet.

snakehead-fish-channidae.context_blurb: The snakehead fish is a family of long, air-breathing predatory fish native to Africa and Asia. They are famous among biologists both for their aggressive hunting behavior in their native rivers and for the environmental damage they can cause when released into waterways where they do not belong. Snakeheads have a trick in their respiratory system that lets them survive out of water for far longer than most fish could ever manage, and they can even cross small stretches of land between pools.

stargazer-uranoscopidae.context_blurb: The stargazer is a group of thickset, bottom-living fish that live buried in sand on continental shelves around the world. They are ambush predators, with eyes and mouths pointed straight up, so that they lie almost flat under the sand and strike at whatever swims directly over them. Stargazers combine several defensive and offensive tricks that very few other fish put together on the same body, including features that make them dangerous to step on.

stonefish-synanceia.context_blurb: The stonefish is a small, lumpy, ugly fish that lives on tropical reefs and rocky shallows across the Indo-Pacific. It is the most venomous fish in the world. Stonefish spend their days half-buried in sand or wedged among coral rubble, where they are nearly invisible. Everything about them, from the texture of their skin to their defensive spines, is a precise solution to the problem of being a slow, chunky fish on a reef full of fast ones.

viperfish-chauliodus.context_blurb:
Far below the surface, in the dark middle layers of warm and temperate oceans, hunts the viperfish: a slender, hand-sized fish with a huge head, a mouthful of needles and a body that can look almost see-through. Food is scarce down there, so the viperfish is built to catch anything it meets and never let it go.

Its fangs are too long to fit inside its mouth, so they curve back until their tips nearly touch its own eyes, and its jaws hang open in a permanent grin. When it lunges and the jaws slam shut, two long front fangs jutting up from the lower jaw close around the victim like the bars of a cage, leaving the prey no way out.

Light is its other weapon. A spine on its back arches forward over its head, tipped with a glowing photophore. The viperfish waves this lure like a fishing pole, flashing it on and off to draw small fish right onto its fangs. Light also hides it. Rows of tiny photophores along its belly glow to match the faint light filtering down from the surface, so a hunter looking up from below sees no dark silhouette, a trick called counter-illumination.

Meals can be days apart, so the viperfish takes whatever it catches, even prey 20 to more than 50 percent bigger than itself. To swallow such a meal, it unhinges its skull, opens its jaws as wide as 90 degrees, and stretches its stomach around the prey. Those inward-curving fangs carry a deadly risk. If a viperfish strikes blind and catches a fish too big to swallow, its teeth hold the meal so fast that it can neither swallow nor spit it out, and it starves.

blanket-octopus-tremoctopus.context_blurb:
The blanket octopus, Tremoctopus, drifts through warm tropical and subtropical seas around the world. The female spreads a shimmering purple web stretched from arm to arm, the "blanket" that gives the animal its name. The species also shows a startling size gap between the sexes, and a weapon no other octopus is known to use.

Unlike most octopuses, which hide in reef crevices and crawl the seafloor, the blanket octopus spends its whole life drifting in open water, from the surface down to about 250 meters, never touching rock or sand. With no shell or reef to hide behind, a female threatened by a tuna unfurls her webbing into a huge iridescent cape, suddenly looking big and frightening enough to warn off tuna, sailfish and even sharks.

It even steals weapons: a blanket octopus tears pieces from the venomous tentacles of a Portuguese man o' war, then holds them in its arms like whips, striking prey and fending off predators with the stolen stingers.

Females reach about 2 meters across, yet a male measures only about 2.4 centimeters, roughly the size of a walnut. To mate, the tiny male packs sperm into a special arm called the hectocotylus, then detaches the whole arm and gives it to the female, and he almost certainly dies soon after.

For centuries the male was known only from dead specimens in trawl nets and plankton samples, until in 2002 Mark Norman and colleagues found the first live adult male off Australia's Great Barrier Reef. In the 1820s naturalists kept finding a squirming thread inside females, and Georges Cuvier described it as a new parasitic worm, Hectocotylus octopodis, but in the 1840s Albert von Kölliker and Heinrich Müller, who found whole dwarf males whose big arm dropped off at a touch, proved the "worm" was the male's own detachable arm, left inside the female after mating.

Only tiny males and small young females have ever been seen carrying man o' war tentacles, never an octopus longer than about 7 centimeters, probably because the larger suckers of a bigger octopus cannot hold such thin stingers without injury. The borrowed weapon may give small males a refuge from predators, and researchers propose that this may itself have pushed females to grow huge while males stayed tiny.

blue-dragon-nudibranch-glaucus-atlanticu.context_blurb:
Glaucus atlanticus, the blue dragon, is a sea slug barely the size of a grape, striped electric blue and silver. It spends its whole life adrift on the warm open ocean, far from any shore or seabed, and this soft little drifter hunts one of the most feared stingers in the sea.

With no shell and almost no power to swim, the slug goes wherever wind and current take it. It rides the surface upside down, belly turned to the sky. It feeds on the Portuguese man o' war, which drifts like a jellyfish and trails tentacles loaded with venomous stinging cells. The slug swallows it, keeps the stingers and concentrates their venom, so the little thief can sting a person even worse than the man o' war it robbed, causing pain, nausea and vomiting.

Those stinging cells, called nematocysts, go down undigested. The slug then sorts them, moving the strongest out of its gut and into its own body, where they wait in its frilly blue arms as borrowed weapons. Scientists call this kleptocnidy, 'stolen stingers.' Its colors guard it against seabirds above and fish below. Because it floats upside down, its counter-shading is reversed: the side facing the sky, its belly, is brilliant blue to vanish against the sea, while the side facing the deep is silver-grey to melt into the bright surface.

For a slug that can barely swim, staying at the top is its own puzzle. The blue dragon swallows a bubble of air and holds it in its stomach, a gas-filled sac that works like a built-in life jacket, helped by the surface tension of the water.

The borrowed stingers outlive the slug: a blue dragon washed up dead on a beach still fires them on contact, so picking up the pretty blue shape can earn a sting. Inside the living slug the weapons are a hazard too, since a few always go off on the way down. It disarms them in two steps: its mucus quiets the stinging cells so fewer fire, and a tough chitin lining, studded with chitin discs called spindles, soaks up any that go off anyway, like sandbags around a blast.

Biologists long saw the blue dragon as a slug that lived on the man o' war and killed with borrowed stings. Then a 2025 aquarium study filmed it catching live small fish, and the stingers played no part. Its front cerata, the fingerlike arms nearest its head, are longer than the rest and muscled at the base. It used them like arms, seizing a fish, pinning it between them and biting near the gills.

blue-ringed-octopus-hapalochlaena.context_blurb:
The blue-ringed octopus, Hapalochlaena, is a golf-ball-sized octopus of tide pools and shallow reefs across the Indo-Pacific, from Australia to Japan. It is easy to miss and is one of the most venomous animals in the sea. Its little body is a kit of warning colors, borrowed chemistry and two kinds of venom, and medical researchers study it closely.

At rest it is a drab gray-brown that melts into the rocks, but when disturbed it flashes dozens of glowing blue rings, a "do not touch" signal that tells predators to keep their distance. It would rather warn than fight, and it bites a person only when it is grabbed or stepped on.

Although it measures only 12 to 20 centimeters including its arms, a single octopus carries enough venom to kill more than 20 adults within minutes. It hunts small crabs, hermit crabs and shrimp by ambush, piercing their shells with a hard, parrot-like beak and injecting paralyzing venom.

The venom is tetrodotoxin, which has no known antidote, the same poison found in the pufferfish, a fish Japanese chefs need a special license to prepare, and in some poison dart frogs and newts; the blue-ringed octopus was the first animal known to use it as a venom. A bite is tiny and painless, but the venom paralyzes the muscles of breathing within minutes, so a rescuer must keep the victim breathing with artificial respiration or a ventilator until the body clears the toxin, usually within about a day. Survive those first 24 hours on breathing support, and recovery is usually complete.

The octopus does not make the poison itself: symbiotic bacteria living in its rear salivary gland manufacture the tetrodotoxin, and the octopus hosts them and delivers their product. It also keeps two different venoms in separate glands, one to subdue prey and the other for defense against predators. Its warning flash is among the fastest color changes in the animal world, 50 to 60 rings in about a third of a second, because the blue comes from inert, mirror-like cells tucked inside skin pouches that muscles snap open, while the surrounding brown cells darken for contrast. In 2025 scientists filmed a close relative, the blue-lined octopus, using venom to mate: the much smaller male bites the female right over the aorta at the back of her head and injects tetrodotoxin, which stops her breathing and leaves her still for 40 to 75 minutes so she cannot eat him, and she recovers fully afterward. It was the first animal known to turn venom into a mating tool.

Why does the octopus not poison itself? Tetrodotoxin works by plugging the sodium channels in nerve and muscle cells, and in 2019 researchers found that the octopus's own channel carries three swapped amino acids that reshape the spot where the toxin docks, so the poison cannot get a grip. Pufferfish, newts and some snakes evolved the same kinds of changes on their own, a striking case of convergent evolution.

bobbit-worm-eunice-aphroditois.context_blurb:
The bobbit worm, Eunice aphroditois, is a long, shimmering sea worm of warm reefs around the world. It spends its life buried in the sand with only its head showing, a living trap that waits for prey to come close. On video its strike looks like a spring-loaded trap snapping shut.

Five thin antennae stick up around its head like fingers, and they work as tripwires: when a fish brushes against one, the hidden worm strikes. Most of its body stays out of sight, but the record specimen stretched 299 centimeters, nearly 10 feet, longer than a grown man lying down, though only about 2.5 centimeters wide.

The strike lasts mere milliseconds, and its scissor-like jaws, serrated and hooked, can sometimes cut a fish clean in half before dragging it under the sand. Once it has hold of prey, it pumps in a toxin that stuns or kills the victim, which lets it subdue and drag down animals far larger than itself.

Staff at Newquay's Blue Reef Aquarium in England saw coral shredded and fish vanishing night after night, and after weeks of empty traps they dismantled the display one rock at a time and found a bobbit worm 1.2 meters long, which they named Barry. When they cornered him, he bit clean through a 20-pound fishing line. Nobody had bought him: Barry arrived as a tiny youngster hidden in a piece of "live rock" the aquarium purchased, then grew unseen for years, ducking into his burrow whenever bright light hit him.

With no limbs to swing its jaws, the worm launches them by turning its muscular throat inside out, flinging the whole jaw apparatus forward like a spring-loaded trap and then pulling it back with the prey. A skeleton of pressurized fluid holds its long body in shape and helps power the launch. Despite its fearsome hunting, it also scavenges algae and dead matter, and it lives only about three to five years.

Soft worms rarely fossilize, but in Taiwanese rock about 20 million years old, Yu-Yen Pan and colleagues found 319 fossils of something the ancient worms left behind: the L-shaped burrows they hunted from, up to 2 meters long and only 2 to 3 centimeters wide. Near the top of each burrow, X-ray scans show a spike of iron left by the worm's mucus, a sign that it rebuilt its lair after every violent strike.

christmas-tree-worm-spirobranchus-gigant.context_blurb:
The Christmas tree worm, Spirobranchus giganteus, is a small marine worm of tropical reefs around the world. It spends its whole life inside a tube in a living coral head, and divers see only its colorful crowns, which handle several jobs at once. Its escape reflex is one of the quickest of any animal without a backbone.

What looks like a pair of tiny, brilliant spiral fir trees in red, blue, orange or yellow is really the two feathery crowns of one worm, which lives head-down in a tube bored into the coral.

Those crowns sit exposed on the reef, so at the slightest touch or even a passing shadow the worm whips them down into its tube in an instant, then creeps back out very slowly about a minute later to test the water. The hair-fringed branches of each crown, called radioles, do double duty: they net drifting plankton and pass it to the mouth, and they also take oxygen from the water like gills, so the worm eats and breathes with the same organ.

Once inside, the worm seals the tube with an operculum, a trapdoor lid reshaped from one of its own crown branches, which plugs the hole while it hides.

The early warning comes from the crown itself, because built into the feathery branches are compound eyes, each with an estimated 600 to 1,000 tiny lenses tuned to the blue light of the reef, which catch the shadow of anything approaching and fire the retreat before the worm is ever touched.

Whether the worm helps its coral is still argued: a 1986 Great Barrier Reef study by DeVantier and colleagues found living coral tissue clustered around the worms where crown-of-thorns starfish were feeding, hinting that the worms may shield their host from those coral-eating starfish, but a 2019 study off Curaçao found the worm's scraping lid often injured the coral instead. The relationship may swing between help and harm from one reef to the next.

coconut-crab-birgus-latro.context_blurb:
The coconut crab, Birgus latro, is a giant hermit crab of tropical islands across the Indian and western Pacific Oceans. It begins life in the sea, spends its adult life on land, climbs palm trees, and on some islands rules as the top predator.

It is the biggest arthropod living on land, spanning more than 3 feet from leg tip to leg tip and weighing up to about 4 kilograms, heavier than a house cat. The coconut crab is also the island animal that can open a coconut, a nut people usually need tools to crack: it climbs the palm, then husks and splits the fruit with its claws over hours of work.

Islanders call it the robber crab because it carries off pots, silverware and shiny objects, and its claws can lift about 29 kilograms. It is a hunter and scavenger too, eating carrion, and on Christmas Island it can tear apart a live red crab in seconds.

In 2016 on Okinawa, Shin-ichiro Oka's team measured the pinch of 29 wild crabs, and the strongest gripped with about 1,765 newtons, more than a lion's canine bite, while the biggest crabs may reach 3,300 newtons, beaten among land predators only by the alligator. Though it starts life in the ocean, an adult's gills have shrunk and it breathes air through a lung-like organ, so it will drown if held underwater. Young coconut crabs, like other hermit crabs, wear borrowed snail shells, but an adult grows too big for any shell and instead hardens the plates of its own abdomen into built-in armor.

Oka himself was pinched twice, and of those few minutes he said, "I felt eternal hell." Its breathing organ, a spongy branchiostegal lung, works only while damp, so the crab strokes water over it with its smallest, hindmost pair of legs and plugs its burrow to keep the air moist. Its larvae drift in the open ocean for three or four weeks, and once a survivor crawls ashore in a snail shell, it can no longer swim, ever. About once a year it molts, burrowing as deep as a meter and plugging the entrance for weeks, and when the old shell slips off, it eats the cast-off shell and reuses its calcium to harden the new armor.

Its sense of smell went its own way: its antennae and the brain region that reads scents came to resemble an insect's rather than a sea crab's, letting it find rotting meat and fruit from far off. On the Chagos Islands, Mark Laidre filmed a crab climbing up to a booby asleep in a tree and breaking its wing, and as rival crabs, drawn within about 20 minutes by the smell of blood, squabbled over the bird for hours, he admitted, "I had a lot of trouble sleeping that night." Laidre also compared three near-identical islands and found that only on the one without coconut crabs did seabirds dare to nest on the ground. In the 1830s Charles Darwin watched one tear a coconut's husk off fibre by fibre, always beginning where the three eye-holes sit, then hammer a claw on an eye-hole until it broke through to the meat. He called it as curious a case of instinct as he had ever heard of. Coconut crabs were the first arthropods tracked by GPS, and when Jakob Krieger's team moved tagged crabs away from home on Christmas Island, most made their way home, ending up a few hundred meters or less from where they were caught, and one retraced its exact outward route, S-bend and all. The team followed 55 crabs between 2008 and 2011, on treks that averaged 1.8 kilometers and reached 4.2, clear evidence of route memory in a crustacean.

teaches.619d1e235e: It is a hunter and scavenger too, eating carrion, and on Christmas Island it can tear apart a live red crab in seconds.

comb-jelly-ctenophora.context_blurb: The comb jelly is a group of transparent, soap-bubble-shaped marine animals found in oceans everywhere, from coastal bays to the deep sea. They are not jellyfish; they are their own ancient branch of the tree of life, and some scientists think they are the oldest surviving animal lineage. Comb jellies swim by beating rows of tiny hair-like plates that run down their bodies, which refract light into shimmering rainbow waves. The animal has no stinging cells and no central brain, yet it hunts actively and in some cases traps prey in sticky cells unique to its group.

dumbo-octopus-grimpoteuthis.context_blurb: The Dumbo octopus is a soft, pale, deep-sea octopus that lives on the sea floor at depths from a few hundred to several thousand meters, in every ocean of the world. It is named for a pair of flaps on top of its mantle that it flaps slowly to swim, which reminded zoologists of the Disney elephant. The Dumbo octopus is much less aggressive than its shallow-water cousins and lives in a cold, dark environment where food is sparse. Everything about it is tuned to that slow, hushed world.

flamboyant-cuttlefish-metasepia-pfefferi.context_blurb: The flamboyant cuttlefish is a small cuttlefish that lives on sandy or muddy seabeds across the tropical Indo-Pacific, from Indonesia to northern Australia. It is only a few inches long, but it is one of the brightest cephalopods on Earth: when disturbed, its skin ripples with a hypnotic display of magenta, yellow, and white. The flamboyant cuttlefish also walks on the sand rather than swims, and the chemistry behind its appearance has its own research literature.

giant-isopod-bathynomus-giganteus.context_blurb: The giant isopod is a deep-sea crustacean that looks like a huge, pale cousin of the common pill bug. It lives on the cold seafloor of the Atlantic and Pacific down to about 2,000 meters. Giant isopods are scavengers, feeding on the sinking bodies of larger animals, and they can go for astonishingly long periods between meals without dying. A famous research aquarium in Japan kept one alive without feeding it for years, which is why the giant isopod has become something of an internet celebrity.

giant-tube-worm-riftia-pachyptila.context_blurb: The giant tube worm is a huge red-tipped worm that lives in dense clusters on the deep ocean floor, especially along the East Pacific Rise. The animal has no mouth, no gut, and no anus. It feeds instead by growing a huge internal community of bacteria inside its own body and sharing chemicals with them in a trade neither partner can run alone. The giant tube worm overturned a huge amount of what biologists thought about where life can live when it was discovered in 1977.

sea-angel-clione.context_blurb: The sea angel is a tiny, transparent sea slug that lives in cold ocean waters, especially around the Arctic and Antarctic. It swims by flapping two wing-like fins that make it look like a floating cherub. Sea angels are predators, and they feed almost exclusively on one specific prey item that they hunt with a surprising piece of equipment. For something that drifts through dark polar seas and looks delicate enough to break, the sea angel is actually a very committed hunter.

vampire-squid-vampyroteuthis-infernalis.context_blurb: The vampire squid is a small, dark, deep-sea cephalopod of the oxygen-minimum layer in warm oceans around the world. Despite its name, it is not a true squid or an octopus; it is the only living member of its own order, with a mix of features from both groups. The vampire squid has webbing between its arms, light-producing patches scattered over its body, and a defensive behavior that makes dramatic use of the webbing. Its diet turned out to be nothing like what people assumed from its name.

venuss-flower-basket-euplectella-aspergi.context_blurb: Venus's flower basket is a deep-sea sponge that lives on the sea floor of the western Pacific. The animal is a hollow, cylindrical cage made of fused glass fibers, and in the dim light of the deep ocean it looks like a woven lantern. The sponge is famous for a specific relationship it has with a pair of shrimp that live trapped inside it for life. The structural engineering of the sponge's glass skeleton is also carefully studied for what it says about building strong materials from brittle parts.

yeti-crab-kiwa.context_blurb: The yeti crab is a group of pale, blind deep-sea crustaceans discovered in 2005 on the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge. The crabs live around hot hydrothermal vents a mile or more below the surface, and their most striking feature is a thick layer of hair-like bristles covering their claws and legs. Those bristles are not just decoration; the yeti crab grows a crop of chemosynthetic bacteria in them that it uses in a very specific way. The animal is one of the clearest living examples of ocean life running on the chemistry of the vents, not sunlight.

club-winged-manakin.context_blurb:
The club-winged manakin, Machaeropterus deliciosus, is a small bird of the wet, mossy cloud forests of western Colombia and Ecuador. The chestnut-brown male wears a bright red cap, and when he courts a female, his whole show is sound. Making that sound reshaped his body and, surprisingly, the female's as well.

He makes a clear, violin-like tone without opening his beak, because he is the only bird known to sing with his wings, rubbing two specially thickened wing feathers together behind his back.

One of those feathers has a shaft lined with a row of ridges like a tiny washboard, and a stiff neighboring feather scrapes across the bumps over a hundred times every second, each bump adding a click that blurs into a pure note. This rub-to-sing method is called stridulation, the same trick a cricket uses, and no other bird is known to do it.

To survive the constant knocking, the male's ulna, a wing bone, is solid and mineralized, nearly three times the volume of a normal bird's, and to the scientists' surprise the silent female carries the same dense, heavy wing bone, so the display reshaped the skeleton of the whole species and made every bird a slightly worse flier.

frogmouth.context_blurb: The frogmouth is a group of nocturnal birds that live in Australia and Southeast Asia. By day, they sit motionless on branches with their beaks pointed upward, blending into the bark so completely that most people will walk right past one without seeing it. Despite the owl-like look and nighttime habits, frogmouths are not owls. They have a huge, frog-shaped mouth they open very wide to catch insects and small prey, and the way they hunt is unlike almost any other bird of their size.

harpy-eagle.context_blurb: The harpy eagle is a huge, powerful eagle that lives in the rainforests of Central and South America. It is one of the largest eagles in the world and the top aerial predator of the Amazon canopy. Harpies hunt from perches rather than from soaring flight, and their talons are built for a very specific kind of prey. The bird is now threatened across much of its range because of deforestation, and conservation projects in Panama and Brazil are trying to protect what is left.

hoatzin.context_blurb: The hoatzin is a strange, pheasant-sized bird that lives in flooded forests along the Amazon and Orinoco rivers of South America. It has a spiky punk-rock crest, a blue face, and a shuffling, clumsy way of moving through the trees. The hoatzin eats almost nothing but leaves, which is almost unheard-of among flying birds, and its gut is more like a cow's than a sparrow's. Its chicks also carry a feature almost no other living bird has.

hoopoe.context_blurb: The hoopoe is a slender, cinnamon-colored bird with a long curved bill and a dramatic black-and-white crest. It lives across Europe, Africa, and much of Asia and spends most of its time on the ground, probing for insects. The hoopoe has turned up in art, poetry, and religious writing from ancient Egypt to the Qur'an, and it is the national bird of Israel. Nesting hoopoes also combine several defensive tricks that have been giving ornithologists material to study for a long time.

kakapo.context_blurb: The kakapo is a huge, flightless, nocturnal parrot that lives only on a few predator-free islands off the coast of New Zealand. There are only about 250 individuals left, each one of them named by biologists. The kakapo is unlike any other parrot: it is heavier than any other, cannot fly, lives on the ground, and breeds only every few years, when a specific food source is abundant. The whole species is one of the most closely managed in the world.

kea.context_blurb: The kea is a large, olive-green parrot that lives only in the mountains of New Zealand's South Island. Keas live where snow sits for much of the year, and they get through that life with a combination of curiosity, playfulness, and problem-solving that puts them in the same mental league as crows and apes. They are also notorious for a specific habit at mountain parking lots that keeps them in the news.

marabou-stork.context_blurb: The marabou stork is a huge, bald-headed scavenging bird that lives across sub-Saharan Africa. It has one of the largest wingspans of any living bird and often weighs more than a human child. The marabou's bare head, huge beak, and dangling throat pouch are the kinds of features that get written into Victorian descriptions as hideous, but each of them is doing a specific job tied to how the bird feeds. Marabou storks are important parts of the African scavenger community.

oilbird.context_blurb: The oilbird is a nocturnal fruit-eating bird that lives in caves in the forested parts of northern South America and Trinidad. It is the only bird in the world that both lives in a cave in deep darkness and also eats only fruit. The oilbird uses a specialized sense to navigate through pitch-black cave passages, which is otherwise mostly associated with bats. Humans once hunted oilbirds for the thick layer of fat on their chicks, which gave the bird its name.

potoo.context_blurb: The potoo is a group of large, nocturnal birds that live in the forests of Central and South America. By day, a potoo sits on a broken-off branch stump with its beak pointed upward and its eyes mostly closed, blending into the stump so perfectly that it looks like part of the tree. At night, it hunts flying insects by diving from its perch and sailing back. The way the potoo spends its day is one of the most reliable camouflage tricks any bird has.

secretarybird.context_blurb: The secretarybird is a tall, long-legged bird of prey that walks across the savannas and grasslands of sub-Saharan Africa. It is unmistakable in silhouette, with the body of an eagle on the legs of a stork. The secretarybird can fly, but it does most of its hunting on foot. Its signature method of killing prey is unusual among raptors and gives it one of the strangest fight styles in the bird world. It is now listed as endangered as its grassland habitat shrinks.

superb-bird-of-paradise.context_blurb: The superb bird-of-paradise is a small, jet-black forest bird that lives in the rainforests of New Guinea. Males put on one of the most carefully choreographed courtship displays in the whole bird world, transforming themselves into a shape and face that look nothing like a normal bird. For a long time the superb bird-of-paradise was treated as one species. Modern DNA work has split it into at least two, each with slightly different dance moves.

sword-billed-hummingbird.context_blurb: The sword-billed hummingbird is a hummingbird that lives in the Andean cloud forests of northern South America. It is the only bird in the world with a bill of its particular shape and proportions. The sword bill is tied closely to a specific set of flowers it feeds from and to a problem of coevolution that keeps turning up in ecology textbooks. The way the bird grooms, perches, and sleeps all has to be adapted around that oversized bill.

toucan.context_blurb:
In the warm rainforests of Central and South America, flocks of toucans move through the canopy, each a black bird carrying a beak so big it looks like a cartoon. That bill is no clumsy ornament. Biologists have found that it is light, handy at mealtimes, and a tool for keeping the bird at the right temperature.

The toucan's brightly colored bill can be four times the size of its head and stretch almost the full length of the rest of the bird.

A toucan plucks fruit with the far end of its bill, well away from its mouth, so to eat it jerks its head back, flips the fruit into the air and catches it as it drops straight down its throat.

Such a beak should weigh the bird down, yet a toucan flies easily. The bill is built like a foam sandwich: a thin outer sheath of keratin, the stuff of fingernails, over an airy core of crisscrossing bony struts and closed, air-filled cells, so it weighs only a tiny fraction of the bird's body. It also works as a radiator the toucan can turn up or down. On hot days the bird sends more blood into its bill to shed heat, losing 30 to 60 percent of its body's heat there, and on cool nights it cuts the flow to hold its warmth in, a 'thermal window' that rivals an elephant's ears.

vulture.context_blurb: Vultures are a group of large scavenging birds that live on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They clean up carcasses that would otherwise rot and spread disease, and the ecosystem job they do is far bigger than most people realize until it stops. Vultures are extremely well equipped for a diet of dead flesh, with chemistry and anatomy tuned to a job no other large bird will take. Several vulture populations around the world have collapsed in the last few decades, and the knock-on effects have been severe.

albatross.context_blurb:
No bird owns the open sea like the wandering albatross, a giant white glider of the stormy Southern Ocean that rings Antarctica. It comes ashore only to breed on remote, windswept islands and spends the rest of its long life on the wing, crossing whole oceans while barely moving a feather. Its secrets lie in its wings, its senses and its unhurried family life.

Tip to tip, its wings span 11 or 12 feet, roughly 3.5 meters, the widest of any bird alive; the record holder measured 3.7 meters. Holding such wings out would exhaust ordinary flight muscles. The albatross does not have to, because a tendon in its shoulder locks each wing straight out like a latch, so the bird can glide for hours with no muscle effort at all.

Its fuel is the wind itself: friction slows the air just above the waves while the air a few dozen meters up races faster, so the albatross climbs into the fast upper air, swoops down into the slow air by the sea and climbs again, harvesting energy from the difference every time. Biologists call this dynamic soaring. With it, a foraging wandering albatross can cover about 950 km in a single day, averaging some 40 km an hour, and keep that pace for days while burning almost no energy. Its meals of squid and small fish come with mouthfuls of seawater, so a salt gland above each eye pulls out the extra salt and concentrates it into brine that drips from the bird's tube-shaped nostrils and down its beak. Those nostrils give albatrosses and their relatives the family nickname "tubenoses." Few birds live so long: a wandering albatross that reaches adulthood can survive 50 to 60 years in the wild, sometimes longer.

Satellite tags show how far all that gliding adds up: a GPS-tracked wandering albatross flew a full loop around Antarctica, about 11,600 km, in just 46 days without landing. Finding food in that emptiness is a puzzle, because squid and krill gather in patches far apart that no eye can spot from the air. When krill graze on tiny drifting plants, the plants give off a gas called dimethyl sulfide, the smell of the ocean, and the albatross catches that scent on the wind and zig-zags upwind toward it, tacking like a sailboat. When Gabrielle Nevitt's team GPS-tagged 19 wandering albatrosses in 2008, those upwind zig-zags led to over a third of daytime catches and nearly half at night, the first hard proof that these birds smell their way to dinner.

Family life runs just as slowly. A pair lays a single egg and incubates it for about 78 days, the longest of any bird, and then the fluffy chick sits on its grassy nest for around 278 days, nearly nine months, before its first flight. Because raising a chick takes so long, a pair breeds only every other year. Partners mate for life, yet between seasons they roam the ocean apart for months. When they meet again at the old nest, the two renew their bond with an elaborate greeting dance of sky-pointing, wing-spreading and loud clucking calls. A smaller Pacific cousin, the Laysan albatross, holds the age record: a female nicknamed Wisdom, banded on Midway Atoll in 1956, is the oldest wild bird known anywhere, more than seventy years old and still raising chicks. She has hatched an estimated thirty or more of them.

Even the albatross's fossil past held a surprise. Giant fossil seabirds from Antarctica with 21-foot wingspans were long filed as the biggest albatrosses that ever flew, since their legs and feet were near copies of an albatross's. Their jaws told the truth: they belonged to a separate lineage, the pelagornithids or "bony-toothed" birds, whose beaks bristled with spikes of bone that looked like teeth. Convergent evolution had shaped their legs alike. Real fossil albatrosses were modest; a 3-million-year-old skull from New Zealand belonged to a bird a little smaller than any albatross alive today.

arctic-tern.context_blurb:
The Arctic tern is a small, slender seabird of cold northern coasts. Each year it breeds in the far north, then flies all the way to Antarctica for the southern summer and back again, chasing the sun from one end of the planet to the other. For decades nobody knew the real length of that commute, until tiny tracking tags revealed it.

It is easy to recognize: a black cap pulled low over the head, white cheeks, a deeply forked tail like a swallow's, and a bill and feet of blood-red. No animal on Earth migrates farther, as a 2010 tracking study by Egevang and colleagues showed: every year the tern flies from its Arctic nesting grounds to Antarctica and back.

Living in summer at both ends of the world, the tern enjoys two summers a year and very likely sees more daylight than any other creature. It does not head straight south but follows a giant S-shaped path down the Atlantic, so its true yearly round trip averages about 70,900 km, roughly 44,000 miles. The birds in the study flew anywhere from 59,500 to 81,600 km in a year. Since a tern can live past 30, a lifetime of these trips adds up to about 2.4 million km, the same as flying to the Moon and back about three times.

That S-shaped path follows each ocean's prevailing winds: the tern swings counterclockwise around the great South Atlantic gyre, and on its way north it circles clockwise around the North Atlantic gyre, instead of fighting a straight crossing. To track a bird weighing roughly 100 grams without burdening it, the researchers fitted 11 terns from Greenland and Iceland with geolocators weighing just 1.4 grams each, attached to their leg bands.

bowerbird.context_blurb:
Bowerbirds are forest birds of Australia and New Guinea, and the males build one of the most elaborate courtship displays in the animal kingdom. On the forest floor each male raises a structure of twigs, a bower, and decorates it with carefully chosen objects to impress visiting females. Their arrangements show real attention to color, pattern and even perspective.

The satin bowerbird's bower, a pair of tidy twig walls side by side, is not a nest at all: the male builds it purely as a stage on which to court females, and he comes back to the same spot year after year. The glossy blue-black male is obsessed with blue, decorating his stage with blue clothes pegs, drinking straws, bottle tops and parrot feathers, a color that matches his own plumage and violet-blue eyes, and he will steal blue objects from as far as 12 kilometers away. A female tours several rival bowers and judges each male's strutting display, and after mating she builds a plain, saucer-shaped nest of sticks as high as 30 to 35 meters up a tree and raises the chicks entirely alone.

He even paints, mashing berries and spit into a purple paint and smearing it on the inside of the walls with a wad of bark held in his beak as a brush. Young males stay drab olive-green like the females for seven years, practicing on scrappy trial bowers, before they finally molt into glossy blue-black adult plumage.

In northern Australia, the male great bowerbird arranges pebbles, shells and bones on the court beyond his avenue in order of size, smallest near the spot where the female stands and largest at the far end, a forced-perspective trick that makes the court look smaller and so makes him look bigger. The golden bowerbird of northeastern Australia builds the tallest bowers of all, twin towers of sticks that a young male inherits and rebuilds on the same spot, and the oldest known bowers are over forty years old and more than 2 meters tall.

cassowary.context_blurb:
The cassowary, a towering bird that cannot fly, lives in the rainforests of northern Australia and New Guinea. It can be dangerous when cornered, yet it is also one of the forest's great gardeners, because a long list of rainforest trees depend on it to spread their seeds.

Standing up to about 2 meters tall, the southern cassowary has glossy black feathers, bright blue skin on its head and neck, red at the back of the neck, and a tall grayish helmet called a casque. Zookeepers who handle ostriches, emus and rheas fear it above all of them, and it is widely called the most dangerous bird in the world; a 2019 death in Florida was the first human fatality blamed on a cassowary in 93 years.

Cornered, it leaps and kicks both feet forward, and each foot's inner toe ends in a dagger-like claw about 12 centimeters, or 5 inches, long that can slash open internal organs.

Chicks trot behind their father, and they hatch striped brown and cream down the back and thighs like little watermelons, camouflage they lose at about three to six months as they turn plain brown.

Deep in the foliage it gives booming calls near 32 hertz, among the lowest sounds known from any bird and right at the bottom of human hearing, probably because such a deep note carries far through thick rainforest where higher calls fade. Its casque may help to send or pick up these calls, though what the helmet is really for is still debated.

emperor-penguin.context_blurb: The emperor penguin is the largest penguin alive, standing about four feet tall. It lives only on the sea ice around Antarctica, which is also where it breeds in the middle of the worst winter on Earth. The emperor penguin raises its single chick through months of darkness and freezing wind by relying on a mix of parental teamwork, group behavior, and body chemistry that nothing else in the vertebrate world comes close to copying.

hummingbird.context_blurb: The hummingbird is a group of tiny, nectar-feeding birds that live only in the Americas. The smallest, the bee hummingbird of Cuba, weighs less than a penny. Hummingbirds have the fastest wingbeats of any bird, hover in place at flowers, and have the highest metabolism of any vertebrate for their size. All of these features drive a specific set of biology problems that hummingbird research keeps unpacking.

kiwi.context_blurb: The kiwi is a group of flightless, chicken-sized birds that live only in New Zealand. They are the national symbol of the country. Kiwis are nocturnal and have soft hair-like feathers, very poor eyesight, and a long flexible bill with nostrils at the tip. The nostrils-at-the-tip trick is almost unique among birds, and they are built around a very different kind of foraging than most of their flying cousins ever use.

lyrebird.context_blurb: The lyrebird is a large, ground-dwelling bird that lives in the forests of eastern Australia. The male has a long tail that fans up like a lyre in display. The lyrebird is one of the greatest vocal mimics in the natural world and can copy almost any sound it hears, including other birds, human machinery, and even camera shutters. The amount and precision of its mimicry is well-documented, and it has made the lyrebird a repeating star of nature documentaries.

new-caledonian-crow.context_blurb: The New Caledonian crow is a medium-sized black crow that lives only on a few islands in the southwest Pacific. It looks like any other crow at first glance, but it is one of the most skilled tool-using animals in the world. Researchers in Oxford and elsewhere have run careful experiments on these crows for decades. The results keep pushing bird cognition into territory most people associate with chimpanzees.

ostrich.context_blurb: The ostrich is the largest living bird on Earth, a flightless runner that lives on the savannas of Africa. An adult male can stand over nine feet tall. Ostriches cannot fly, but they can run faster than any other bird and defend themselves with a powerful kick. Their eggs, their eyes, and their lungs are all record-setters in their own ways. Ostriches are also still farmed in a number of countries for meat, leather, and feathers.

owl.context_blurb: The owl is a group of mostly nocturnal birds of prey found in every habitat on every continent except Antarctica. Owls combine almost silent flight, forward-facing eyes, and an extraordinary sense of hearing to hunt in near-total darkness. Each of those abilities depends on a specific anatomical feature not shared by most daytime raptors. Species of owl range from palm-sized elf owls to the Blakiston's fish owl, which has a wingspan close to six feet.

peregrine-falcon.context_blurb: The peregrine falcon is a widespread bird of prey found on every continent except Antarctica. It is best known for its hunting dive, which uses gravity to reach some of the fastest speeds ever measured in a living animal. Peregrines nearly went extinct across much of North America in the mid-twentieth century because of DDT contamination; they are now one of the most famous success stories of modern conservation. City skyscrapers in New York, Chicago, and London are now important peregrine nest sites.

shoebill.context_blurb: The shoebill is a huge, slate-grey wading bird that lives in the papyrus swamps of central and eastern Africa. It is one of the tallest wading birds in the world and has a gigantic shoe-shaped bill, from which it gets its name. Shoebills hunt by standing almost perfectly still for hours and then striking in a single motion that biologists have measured carefully. They are also famous for a specific sound they make instead of a call, and for a disturbing look at anyone who gets too close to their nest.

woodpecker.context_blurb: Woodpeckers are a group of birds found in forests on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They are specialized tree-poundingclimbers with chisel-like beaks, stiff tails, and feet built for gripping bark. Woodpeckers hammer into wood at speeds and forces that would knock out any other bird's brain, and the way they manage to not get hurt is one of the most carefully studied puzzles in avian biomechanics.

17-year-cicada.context_blurb:
In the eastern United States, the forest floor can lie quiet for seventeen years and then, in one summer, boil with insects. Periodical cicadas spend nearly their whole lives in the dark soil and surface by the billions at once, staking their survival on timing and sheer numbers.

The periodical cicada is unforgettable once seen: a glossy black body as long as your thumb, two bulging eyes as red as coals, and clear wings veined in bright orange. For about 99.5 percent of its life it is a pale nymph underground, feeding on the sap of tree roots for 13 or 17 years. Then a whole brood climbs out together in the same few days. Biologists call this survival trick, safety in overwhelming numbers, predator satiation.

The nymphs seem to count the years by sensing seasonal changes in the sap of the roots, then wait for one last cue: the soil about eight inches down warming to roughly 64°F. Out they come, and the males begin to sing. Each male snaps a stiff, ribbed membrane on either side of his body, the tymbal, so fast that the clicks blur together. His abdomen is hollow, and that empty chamber resonates like the body of a guitar, swelling the clicks into a roar of about 100 decibels, among the loudest calls of any insect. After all those years in the dark, an adult lives just four to six weeks above ground, long enough to sing, mate and lay eggs.

A cicada cannot sting, hide or outrun anything, so its defense is arithmetic. A single acre can hold more than 1.5 million of them. Birds and foxes gorge until they can eat no more, and still most of the brood survives to mate. Even the length of the wait may be a weapon, because 13 and 17 are prime numbers, divisible only by themselves and one. As the entomologists Monte Lloyd and Henry Dybas proposed in 1966, a predator whose numbers peak every two, three or four years will almost never peak in the same summer a prime-numbered brood appears, while a 12-year brood would meet all of those hunters at full strength. Stephen Jay Gould later made the idea famous, though it remains a leading hypothesis, not a proven fact.

army-ants.context_blurb:
Army ants live in the tropical forests of the Americas, Africa and Asia, and they never settle down. Instead of building a permanent nest, a whole colony marches through the forest in long columns, overwhelming prey far too big for any single ant. In Central and South American rainforests, Eciton burchellii sends out raids of hundreds of thousands of workers at once.

When the march halts for the night, the workers hook their feet together and become the nest themselves, a living shelter called a bivouac that walls in the queen and the young.

Remarkably, the workers that steer a raid are blind or nearly so, and they hold the swarm together by touch and by chemical scent trails, called pheromones, that they lay down with their own bodies. When a column meets a gap, such as a split between two leaves, ants hook together with the claws on their feet and span it with their bodies, a living bridge the raid pours straight across without slowing.

When Scott Powell and Nigel Franks set out planks full of holes of different sizes on a raiding trail, each worker picked a hole that matched its own body size and flattened into it, so ants carrying prey could run home at full speed over a road paved with their nestmates. Even a nest made only of ants has climate control: the colony opens and closes air passages through the cluster, holding its core near 28.5°C while the air outside heats and cools.

bombardier-beetle.context_blurb:
Barely half an inch long, the bombardier beetle is a ground beetle of fields and forests on every continent except Antarctica. It carries one of the most dramatic chemical weapons in the animal kingdom, blasted out of its hind end and aimed in almost any direction, and scientists still study the chemistry behind the blast.

Grab one and it fires back with a loud pop: a jet of scalding chemical spray, shot from its rear, that makes the attacker drop it at once. The jet comes out near 100°C, or 212°F, as hot as boiling water, enough to scald an attacker's mouth or feet.

The beetle stays safe from its own weapon by storing the two ingredients, hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone, in separate reservoirs and letting them meet only at the instant it fires. In a lab experiment, faint pops sounded from inside toads that had swallowed bombardier beetles, and 43 percent of the toads threw the beetle back up, after it had spent anywhere from 12 to 107 minutes inside; the slimy beetles scuttled away, and nearly all survived, one for at least 562 more days.

The ingredients meet in a reinforced chamber lined with the enzymes catalase and peroxidase, which make the reaction so fast and hot that it boils and blasts outward. High-speed photography showed that the spray is not a steady stream but a pulse jet of about 70 tiny explosions fired at roughly 500 a second, and the pulsing protects the beetle, since each blast escapes before the next builds up, so the chamber never overloads.

dragonfly.context_blurb: The dragonfly is a group of long-bodied flying insects that live near fresh water on every continent except Antarctica. The adults are expert fliers that can hover, dart, and reverse in a way no other insect family can match. Dragonflies spend most of their lives as aquatic larvae, which are themselves fierce underwater predators. Everything about the dragonfly, from its eyes to its wings to its hunting strategy, is tuned for catching other flying insects in open air.

dung-beetle.context_blurb: The dung beetle is a group of beetles that eat the droppings of larger animals and roll them into balls for food and breeding. They live on every continent except Antarctica. Dung beetles play a huge role in recycling nutrients in grasslands and farms around the world, and the ancient Egyptians treated them as sacred. Modern research keeps finding surprising things about how a dung beetle rolling a ball of dung knows where it is going.

firefly.context_blurb: The firefly is a kind of beetle that produces its own light in a pair of chemical-filled segments at the end of its abdomen. Fireflies live in warm, humid parts of every continent except Antarctica. On warm summer evenings, males fly over fields and forests flashing a species-specific pattern, while females wait in the grass and flash back. Modern biologists study the chemistry of firefly light for both its evolutionary story and its use in medical research.

hercules-beetle.context_blurb: The Hercules beetle is a huge rhinoceros beetle that lives in the rainforests of Central and South America. Males grow long, curved horns on their heads and bodies, which can be nearly as long as the rest of them. The Hercules beetle is one of the strongest animals on Earth relative to its body weight, and biologists sometimes use it as a benchmark when they are measuring how much an insect of a given size can lift or drag.

honeybee.context_blurb: The honeybee is a small, striped flying insect that lives in large colonies of thousands of workers, a handful of drones, and a single queen. The common honeybee was first domesticated in the Mediterranean thousands of years ago and is now kept all over the world. Honeybees are the most important crop pollinator of modern agriculture, and the way the colony makes decisions as a group, finds food, and defends its hive has made them one of the most carefully studied insects on Earth.

leafcutter-ants.context_blurb: Leafcutter ants are a group of ants that live in the tropical forests of Central and South America. They are famous for marching columns of workers each carrying a cut piece of leaf back to the nest. The ants do not actually eat the leaves. Instead, they use them to grow a crop in underground chambers, and the colony arrangement around that crop is one of the most striking cases of farming anywhere outside the human world.

monarch-butterfly.context_blurb: The monarch butterfly is a large orange-and-black butterfly that lives across North America, with populations in Mexico, the United States, and Canada. It is best known for one of the most famous animal migrations on Earth, a multi-generation journey between winter roost sites in central Mexico and summer breeding grounds far to the north. Monarchs are also chemically defended as caterpillars, and both of those features are at the heart of modern conservation efforts to save a species that has been declining fast.

peacock-spider.context_blurb: The peacock spider is a group of tiny jumping spiders that live mostly in Australia. The males fit on a fingernail, but they put on an elaborate visual courtship display that has made them an internet sensation. The dance is complicated enough that researchers have mapped out individual moves. For a species this small, the show is extraordinary.

praying-mantis.context_blurb: The praying mantis is a group of long, slender predatory insects found across most of the world, especially the tropics. They are named for the way they hold their folded forelegs together as they wait in ambush for other insects. Mantises have forward-facing eyes, extremely fast strike reflexes, and a famous courtship pattern that often makes it into high-school biology classrooms. They are the only insects that can turn their heads to look over their shoulders.

tardigrade.context_blurb: The tardigrade, also called a water bear or moss piglet, is a microscopic eight-legged animal that lives in mosses, lichens, and water puddles almost everywhere on Earth. Tardigrades are famous for surviving conditions that would kill almost any other animal, including the vacuum of space, deep radiation, and complete dehydration. The way they manage all this is still being worked out, and researchers have launched tardigrades on space missions on purpose to test the limits.

axolotl.context_blurb:
The axolotl is a soft, pale-pink salamander with black eyes and a frilly crown, found in the wild only in the old lake canals of Mexico City. Millions live in laboratories and home aquariums around the world, because the axolotl does two things almost no other animal can: it keeps a baby-like body all its life, and it rebuilds lost body parts.

Its frilly crown is made of six feathery branches fanning out behind its head, and they are external gills: oxygen passes straight from the water into the blood flowing through them. Its famous grin says nothing about its mood; the smile is simply the fixed, upturned shape of its mouth.

The axolotl never grows up in the usual way: it keeps its feathery gills, soft body and tail fin for life, yet it becomes fully mature and breeds while still in that larval form, a condition biologists call neoteny. It is also a champion of regrowth: if a tankmate bites off a leg, a complete new leg grows back within weeks, with bone, muscle, nerves, blood vessels and even the pigment pattern, and no scar. Yet in the wild it is critically endangered: pollution and sewage cut the population by 99 percent between 1998 and 2014, and perhaps 50 to 1,000 survive, all in the canals of Xochimilco, the last scrap of the great lakes that once surrounded Mexico City.

Legs are only the start, because the axolotl can also regrow its tail, its jaw, sections of its spinal cord, portions of its brain and even parts of its heart. The secret lies in how a wound heals: a human cut closes with a patch of collagen that toughens into scar tissue, but an axolotl stump clears away the debris and then switches its cells back into embryo-style growth, rebuilding the part perfectly. Its immune system is unusually tolerant, too: scientists have grafted eyes and even pieces of brain from one axolotl onto another, and the foreign organs settled in and worked normally, with no rejection. Its baby form can even be undone: given thyroid hormone, an axolotl loses its gills, its tail fin shrinks, and it crawls onto land as a gill-less salamander that looks almost exactly like its cousin the tiger salamander.

In a 1968 experiment reported in the journal Science, researchers grafted a second head onto an axolotl, and the extra head not only survived but grew and behaved like a normal head, snapping at and eating prey on its own. Regrowth depends on the immune system: in 2013 Godwin, Pinto and Rosenthal wiped out an axolotl's macrophages, a type of immune cell, before amputating a limb, and the stump healed like a mammal's wound, sealed for good under thick collagen scar tissue, so no leg ever grew back, even after the macrophages returned.

When scientists read its genome in 2018, it was the largest ever assembled, about 32 billion letters, more than ten times the human genome, and it held a shock: Pax3, a gene every other backboned animal was thought to need, is missing, and its close cousin gene Pax7 has taken over the job.
